The critical legal question for QSBS preservation in the CV transaction is whether the transfer of QSBS from Fund II to the CV preserves the stock\'s QSBS character and permits tacking of the holding period. Section 1202(h) addresses this question in part but does not expressly cover all of the transactional steps involved.

> • **Section 1202(h)(4)(A) --- Partnership Distributions:** QSBS distributed by a partnership to a partner retains its QSBS character, and the partner tacks the partnership\'s holding period. This is the provision most directly relevant to the first step of the recommended two-step approach (Fund II distributing shares to the Rolling LPs).

*Step One: Fund II Distributes Shares to Rolling LPs.* Under Section 1202(h)(4)(A), when a partnership distributes QSBS to a partner, the distributed stock retains its QSBS character in the hands of the distributee partner, and the partner\'s holding period includes the partnership\'s holding period. This provision clearly applies to the first step of the recommended approach. After the distribution, each Rolling LP will hold QSBS shares with a tacked holding period that includes Fund II\'s holding period (dating back to the original issuance dates in 2020 and 2021).

> \(iii\) The legislative history of Section 1202 reflects a policy of encouraging long-term investment in small businesses. The contribution of QSBS to a partnership is an intermediate step that facilitates continued holding --- exactly the type of transaction that Section 1202 was designed to encourage.

**Step Transaction Doctrine Risk.** There is a risk that the IRS could seek to collapse the two-step distribution/contribution into a single integrated transaction under the step transaction doctrine, arguing that the distribution from Fund II and the contribution to the CV were mutually dependent steps with no independent economic significance. To mitigate this risk, we recommend:

> \(a\) Ensuring that each step has independent legal and economic significance --- the distribution from Fund II should be documented as a bona fide distribution under the Fund II LPA, and the contribution to the CV should be documented as a separate contribution agreement.
> \(b\) Allowing a reasonable time interval between the two steps (even a short period of days) to demonstrate that they are not simultaneously executed.

> \(c\) Documenting the independent business purposes of each step --- the distribution serves to wind down Fund II\'s holding of the portfolio company shares, and the contribution serves to capitalize the CV.

**Alternative Approach: Single-Step Contribution.** If the two-step approach is determined to be impractical or is disfavored for non-tax reasons, the alternative is a single-step Section 721 contribution directly from Fund II to the CV. This approach is more administratively efficient but, as discussed above, relies on a less well-established legal basis for QSBS tacking. We do not recommend this approach as the primary structure, but we note that it is a viable alternative with a reasonable (though less certain) basis for QSBS preservation.

**Vectral-Specific Consideration.** Because Vectral\'s five-year QSBS holding period does not expire until March 2026, any disposition of the Vectral shares before that date would result in the loss of QSBS eligibility. We recommend including a specific holding covenant in the Tax Protection Agreement that prohibits the CV from disposing of the Vectral shares before March 2026, absent the written consent of a supermajority of the Rolling LPs. This covenant should be enforceable by the Rolling LPs and should include appropriate remedies (including indemnification for lost QSBS benefits) in the event of a breach.

This non-conformity is a significant cost for California taxpayers in the fund. Given that Fund II and Pinnacle Capital Management LLC are California entities, and that the GP principals (Marcus Aldren, Diana Tsao, and Rafael Montoya) are presumed to be California residents, the California tax exposure on the GP carry and co-invest is substantial. For non-California LPs, the exposure depends on whether the gain from the disposition of the portfolio company shares is characterized as California-source income, which in turn depends on the commercial domicile and activities of the CV and the portfolio companies within California. Luminos Systems, headquartered in San Francisco, creates significant California nexus. We address state tax considerations in greater detail in Section X.

> 1\. **Proceed with the two-step distribution/contribution approach** as the primary recommendation for transferring the portfolio company shares from Fund II to the CV, in order to maximize the applicability of the Section 1202(h)(4)(A) safe harbor for QSBS tacking.

> 2\. **Obtain QSBS eligibility certifications** from each portfolio company CEO (Priya Venkatesh for Luminos, Jonathan Hargrove for ClearArc, and Elena Kowalski for Vectral) confirming: (a) the company\'s status as a domestic C-corporation; (b) the aggregate gross assets at the time of each issuance of QSBS to Fund II; (c) compliance with the active business requirement during the relevant holding period; and (d) the absence of any disqualifying events.

> 3\. **Include QSBS representation and covenant provisions** in the CV LPA, including representations by the GP regarding the QSBS eligibility of the portfolio company shares and covenants by the GP to use commercially reasonable efforts to maintain the portfolio companies\' compliance with the Section 1202 requirements.

> 4\. **Include a Vectral holding covenant** in the Tax Protection Agreement, prohibiting the CV from disposing of the Vectral shares before March 2026 (the five-year QSBS holding period maturity date) without the written consent of a supermajority of the Rolling LPs.
**B. Fund II Existing Carry**

Fund II\'s carried interest is structured as a 20% carry over an 8% preferred return (compounded annually) with a 100% GP catch-up. The carried interest has been held by Pinnacle Capital Partners II LLC (Fund II\'s GP) and the GP principals since the fund\'s final close in December 2019. The Section 1061 three-year holding period was therefore satisfied as of December 2022. All gains currently allocated to the Fund II carried interest qualify for long-term capital gain treatment under Section 1061, provided that the underlying portfolio companies have been held by Fund II for more than three years (which is the case for all three portfolio companies --- the most recent investment, Vectral, was made in March 2021, more than four years ago).
We recommend that the GP\'s existing Fund II carried interest be rolled into the CV as a \"legacy carry\" tranche, preserving the economics and, critically, the holding period of the Fund II carry.

**Mechanics.** The rollover will be structured as a Section 721 contribution. Pinnacle Capital Partners II LLC (or the individual GP principals, depending on the precise structuring) will contribute its Fund II carried interest to the CV in exchange for the legacy carry interest in the CV. This contribution qualifies for non-recognition treatment under Section 721(a), and the GP\'s holding period in the CV legacy carry tranche will include the holding period of the Fund II carried interest under Section 1223(1) --- dating back to December 2019.

**Result.** The legacy carry tranche in the CV will inherit the Fund II holding period. Because the Section 1061 three-year holding period was already satisfied as of December 2022, gains allocated to the legacy carry tranche should qualify for long-term capital gain treatment immediately upon CV closing. This is a significant benefit, as it avoids the three-year waiting period that would apply to newly issued carried interest.

**Risk.** There is a risk that the IRS could argue that the CV constitutes a \"new\" partnership interest, rather than a rollover of the existing Fund II interest, thereby resetting the Section 1061 holding period. To mitigate this risk, we recommend:
> \(b\) Ensuring that the LPA provisions describing the legacy carry tranche expressly reference the Fund II carried interest and its original holding period.
> \(c\) Maintaining contemporaneous documentation establishing the continuity between the Fund II carry and the CV legacy carry.
> \(d\) Ensuring that the Section 721 contribution of the carry interest is properly documented and that the carrying amounts are consistent between Fund II and the CV.

In addition to the legacy carry tranche, the GP will be entitled to a new carried interest in the CV on the terms described in Section III.B (15% over 7% preferred return, European-style waterfall). This new carry constitutes a newly issued API with a holding period commencing at the CV closing (estimated October 31, 2025).

The Section 1061 three-year holding period for the new CV carry will not be satisfied until **October 31, 2028** (three years after closing). Any gains allocated to the new carry tranche before that date will be recharacterized as short-term capital gain, taxed at ordinary income rates of up to 37% federal (plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, for a combined federal rate of up to 40.8%).

> • If all three portfolio companies were sold at their current FMV immediately after closing, the GP\'s new carry on the \$1.202 billion of built-in gain would generate significant short-term capital gain. However, this is unlikely given the CV\'s five-year term.

Each principal\'s API holding period is tracked independently. All three principals have held the Fund II carried interest since December 2019 and therefore have a legacy carry holding period of approximately five years and eight months as of the date of this memorandum. The new carry holding period for each principal will commence at the CV closing date.

Capital gains on the GP co-invest are subject to the standard one-year holding period for long-term capital gain treatment, not the Section 1061 three-year requirement. Under Section 1223(1), the GP\'s holding period in the co-invest will begin at the CV closing date (October 31, 2025), and the standard one-year holding period will be satisfied by November 2026.

It is critical that the LPA clearly delineate the GP co-invest capital accounts from the carry interests. Section 1061(c)(4)(A) provides that an API does not include a capital interest that provides the holder a right to share in partnership capital commensurate with the amount of capital contributed or the fair market value of any assets contributed. To preserve this exclusion, the co-invest capital accounts must be maintained separately, and the capital gains attributable to the co-invest must be tracked independently from the carry allocations.
**G. LPA Drafting Recommendations**
We recommend the following provisions be included in the CV LPA to address Section 1061 compliance:

> 3\. **Section 1061 reporting provisions.** The LPA should include provisions requiring the partnership to report API-related information on each partner\'s Schedule K-1, consistent with the reporting requirements under Section 1061 and the regulations thereunder.

> 5\. **Coordination with Hawthorne Reid LLP.** We will provide Hawthorne Reid LLP with a markup of the relevant LPA provisions to ensure that the carried interest bifurcation and Section 1061 compliance mechanisms are properly reflected in the governing documents.

The CV\'s investor base includes two categories of investors for whom direct partnership investment in the CV would create adverse tax consequences: (a) U.S. tax-exempt investors and (b) non-U.S. investors. The blocker entity architecture is designed to interpose corporate entities between these investors and the CV, thereby \"Blocking\" the flow-through of certain categories of income that would otherwise create tax liabilities or compliance burdens for these investors.

**Formation Timeline.** We recommend forming the Domestic blocker by September 30, 2025, in advance of the CV\'s first close on October 15, 2025, to ensure the entity is in place and properly capitalized at closing.

> *Single Combined blocker.* A single blocker entity serving both tax-exempt and non-U.S. investors is theoretically possible but is not recommended due to the different tax regimes applicable to each investor class. The Domestic blocker is designed to block UBTI for tax-exempt U.S. entities, while the Offshore blocker is designed to block ECI and FIRPTA for non-U.S. entities. Combining these functions in a single entity would create unnecessary complexity in the entity\'s U.S. and non-U.S. tax reporting and could compromise the effectiveness of the blocking function for one or both investor classes.

3456: **[II. Background and Transaction Overview]{.underline}**
3457: 
3458: **[A. The Continuation Vehicle]{.underline}**
3459: 
3460: Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP (\"Fund II\") is a Delaware limited partnership (EIN: 84-3291067) formed for the purpose of making venture capital investments in early-stage and growth-stage technology companies. Fund II is managed by Pinnacle Capital Management LLC (EIN: 82-6140538), a Delaware limited liability company headquartered at 2100 Sand Hill Road, Suite 340, Menlo Park, California 94025. The general partner entity of Fund II is Pinnacle Capital Partners II LLC (EIN: 84-3291104), a Delaware limited liability company.
3461: 
3462: Fund II is a 2019 vintage fund. Its final close occurred in December 2019, with total committed capital of \$875 million. As of the date of this memorandum, called capital stands at approximately \$831.25 million, representing a 95% draw-down ratio. Based on the audited financials prepared by Andover & Strauss LLP as of June 30, 2025, Fund II\'s gross net asset value (\"NAV\") is approximately \$1.82 billion, and its net NAV (after deduction of accrued carried interest, management fees, and fund expenses) is approximately \$1.56 billion. Fund II has generated strong returns since inception, driven principally by the appreciation of its three largest portfolio company positions, which collectively represent the substantial majority of fund value.
3463: 
3464: The CV --- to be formed as Pinnacle Continuation Vehicle LP, a Delaware limited partnership --- will hold three concentrated portfolio company stakes to be transferred from Fund II. These positions, which represent the highest-conviction, longest-duration assets in Fund II\'s portfolio, are as follows:
3465: 
3466: **Luminos Systems Inc.** Luminos Systems Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation (EIN: 47-8823156) engaged in the development and commercialization of enterprise-grade artificial intelligence and machine learning infrastructure software. As of June 30, 2025, the fair market value of Fund II\'s interest in Luminos is approximately \$612 million, against a cost basis of \$58.5 million, representing unrealized appreciation of \$553.5 million. Fund II holds approximately 24.7% of Luminos on a fully diluted basis. Luminos is headquartered in San Francisco, California.
3467: 
3468: **ClearArc Software Inc.** ClearArc Software Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation (EIN: 83-5519274) specializing in cybersecurity and data compliance solutions for regulated financial institutions. The fair market value of Fund II\'s interest in ClearArc as of June 30, 2025 is approximately \$468 million, against a cost basis of \$37.4 million, representing unrealized appreciation of \$430.6 million. Fund II holds approximately 31.2% of ClearArc on a fully diluted basis. ClearArc is headquartered in Austin, Texas.
3469: 
3470: **Vectral Cloud Inc.** Vectral Cloud Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation (EIN: 85-1102847) engaged in the provision of hybrid cloud infrastructure and edge computing services. The fair market value of Fund II\'s interest in Vectral as of June 30, 2025 is approximately \$260 million, against a cost basis of \$42.1 million, representing unrealized appreciation of \$217.9 million. Fund II holds approximately 18.9% of Vectral on a fully diluted basis. Vectral is headquartered in Denver, Colorado.
3471: 
3472: In the aggregate, the three portfolio company positions have a combined fair market value of \$1.34 billion and a combined cost basis of \$138 million, resulting in total unrealized built-in gain of \$1.202 billion. The implied gross multiple on invested capital (\"MOIC\") for the three positions is approximately 9.71×.
3473: 
3474: The transfer of the three portfolio company interests from Fund II to the CV will be structured as a contribution under Section 721 of the Code, which provides for non-recognition of gain or loss on contributions of property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. The Section 721 contribution will give rise to the Section 704(c) built-in gain allocations discussed in detail in Section VIII of this memorandum and in the companion Section 704(c) Allocation Methodology Memo.
3475: 
3476: **[B. CV Capitalization]{.underline}**
3477: 
3478: The CV will be capitalized from three sources:
3479: 
3480: **Rolling LPs.** Existing limited partners of Fund II who elect to roll their interests into the CV (rather than cash out) will contribute approximately \$680 million in NAV to the CV. These rolling LPs include, among others, Meridian Public Employees\' Retirement System, Ashford University Endowment, and Sovereign Capital Partners (Cayman) Ltd. --- the three investors who are the subjects of this memorandum --- as well as various other institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals who are not expected to require blocker structures.
3481: 
3482: **New Secondary Capital.** Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP, a secondary buyer vehicle managed by Garrison Capital Advisors LLC, will commit \$380 million of new capital as the lead secondary buyer in the transaction. Garrison\'s commitment represents the principal source of fresh capital for the CV. The primary contact at Garrison is Mitchell Adler, Partner. Garrison\'s outside legal counsel is Whitfield & Calloway LLP, with Douglas Whitfield, Partner, serving as lead outside counsel.
3483: 
3484: **GP Co-Investment.** Pinnacle Capital Management LLC and its principals will make a co-investment of \$14 million into the CV, consistent with standard general partner co-investment practices.
3485: 
3486: Total CV capitalization at close is projected to be \$1.074 billion. Of the \$380 million in Garrison secondary capital, approximately \$280 million will be used to provide liquidity to Fund II limited partners who elect to cash out of the continuation vehicle transaction. The remaining \$100 million will be designated for follow-on investment reserves and fund-level expenses.
3487: 
3488: The CV will be formed as a Delaware limited partnership, Pinnacle Continuation Vehicle LP, with a new general partner entity, Pinnacle CV Partners LLC, to be formed as a Delaware limited liability company. Hawthorne Reid LLP (Vanessa Liu, Partner) is serving as fund formation counsel and is responsible for preparing the limited partnership agreement and related formation documents.
3489: 
3490: The proposed economics of the CV are as follows: a management fee of 1.25% per annum calculated on net asset value; carried interest of 15% over a 7% annual preferred return calculated on a European-style (whole-fund) waterfall basis; and a fund term of five years from the date of the final close, subject to two one-year extension periods at the discretion of the general partner, in each case subject to the consent of the LP advisory committee.
3491: 
3492: **[C. Investors Requiring blocker Protection]{.underline}**
3493: 
3494: Three limited partners of Fund II, each of which is electing to roll 100% of its existing Fund II interests into the CV, have been identified as requiring blocker entity protection for U.S. federal income tax purposes. The relevant characteristics of each investor are summarized below.
3495: 
3496: **Meridian Public Employees\' Retirement System.** Meridian is a U.S. tax-exempt public pension fund qualifying for exemption from U.S. federal income tax under Sections 501(a) and 401(a) of the Code. Meridian\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$125 million, and it is electing a 100% rollover of its Fund II interest into the CV. The primary contact at Meridian is Trevor Huang, Chief Investment Officer. Meridian has expressed a high degree of sensitivity to any structural arrangement that could result in the recognition of UBTI, and its investment committee approval for participation in the CV is conditioned on the availability of UBTI-blocking protection.
3497: 
3498: **Ashford University Endowment.** Ashford is a U.S. tax-exempt educational endowment qualifying for exemption from U.S. federal income tax under Section 501(c)(3) of the Code. Ashford\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$50 million, and it is likewise electing a 100% rollover into the CV. The primary contact at Ashford is Camille Berger, Director of Investments. Like Meridian, Ashford has a high sensitivity to UBTI exposure and requires blocker protection as a condition of its continued participation.
3499: 
3500: **Sovereign Capital Partners (Cayman) Ltd.** Sovereign Capital is a Cayman Islands exempted company that serves as a non-U.S. feeder vehicle for a consortium of Asian family offices. Sovereign Capital\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$75 million, and it is electing a 100% rollover into the CV. The primary contact is Kenneth Fong, Managing Director. Sovereign Capital has expressed a high degree of sensitivity to exposure to U.S. effectively connected income, FIRPTA withholding, and the administrative burden of direct U.S. income tax return filing obligations.
3501: 
3502: **[III. The Need for blocker Structures]{.underline}**
3503: 
3504: **[A. UBTI Concerns for Tax-Exempt Investors]{.underline}**
3505: 
3506: Organizations that qualify for exemption from U.S. federal income tax under Section 501(a) of the Code --- including pension funds qualifying under Section 401(a) (such as Meridian) and educational and charitable organizations qualifying under Section 501(c)(3) (such as Ashford) --- are generally exempt from U.S. federal income tax on their investment income. This exemption, however, is subject to a significant exception: tax-exempt organizations are subject to tax on UBTI as defined in Section 512 of the Code.
3507: 
3508: UBTI is broadly defined to include gross income derived by an exempt organization from any unrelated trade or business regularly carried on by the organization, less the deductions directly connected with the carrying on of such trade or business. The UBTI rules are designed to prevent tax-exempt organizations from enjoying a competitive advantage over taxable enterprises by conducting commercial activities under the umbrella of their tax-exempt status.
3509: 
3510: Several features of the CV structure create potential UBTI exposure for Meridian and Ashford if they were to invest directly as limited partners in the CV:
3511: 
3512: **Debt-Financed Income (Section 512(b)(4)).** Under Section 512(b)(4) of the Code, income derived from debt-financed property is treated as UBTI to the extent that such property is financed with \"acquisition indebtedness\" as defined in Section 514. If the CV were to incur borrowings --- whether through a subscription-line credit facility, a leveraged co-investment alongside a portfolio company, or other forms of fund-level or investment-level indebtedness --- the income allocable to the debt-financed portion of the CV\'s investments would constitute UBTI to Meridian and Ashford. This risk is particularly acute in the present context because the CV\'s \$100 million follow-on reserve may be supplemented by borrowings to finance additional investments in the three portfolio companies, and the CV may also enter into a subscription credit facility to manage the timing of capital calls and distributions.
3513: 
3514: **Income from Partnership Interests (Section 512(c)).** Under Section 512(c), a tax-exempt organization that is a partner in a partnership is treated as having derived its allocable share of the partnership\'s gross income from an unrelated trade or business, to the extent the partnership itself is engaged in such a trade or business. While the CV\'s primary activity --- holding equity interests in portfolio companies structured as C-corporations --- does not itself constitute an unrelated trade or business, the CV\'s ancillary activities (such as providing management consulting services to portfolio companies, if applicable) could give rise to UBTI allocable to its partners.
3515: 
3516: **Interaction of UBTI and Partnership Allocations.** More generally, because the CV is structured as a pass-through entity for U.S. federal income tax purposes, any item of income, gain, deduction, or loss recognized at the partnership level flows through to the partners in accordance with their distributive shares under the limited partnership agreement. To the extent any such item constitutes UBTI, it retains that character in the hands of the tax-exempt partners. This includes not only operating income and debt-financed income, but also certain categories of fee income and other amounts that may be treated as UBTI under the broad definitional framework of Section 512.
3517: 
3518: If Meridian (\$125 million) and Ashford (\$50 million) were to hold their CV interests directly, they would be exposed to UBTI on: (i) debt-financed portfolio income to the extent the CV or any blocker-equivalent intermediate entity utilizes leverage, (ii) any operating income allocations from portfolio companies to the extent structured as pass-through entities (though the three current portfolio companies are C-corporations, there is no guarantee that the CV will not make follow-on investments in entities organized as partnerships or LLCs), and (iii) certain fee-related income. The magnitude of this exposure could be substantial, particularly if the CV utilizes leverage in connection with follow-on investments from the \$100 million reserve.
3519: 
3520: **[B. ECI and FIRPTA Concerns for Non-U.S. Investors]{.underline}**
3521: 
3522: Non-U.S. investors who hold interests in a U.S. partnership that is engaged in a U.S. trade or business face a distinct but equally significant set of adverse U.S. federal income tax consequences.
3523: 
3524: **Effectively Connected Income (Sections 871(b) and 882(a)).** Under Sections 871(b) and 882(a) of the Code, a nonresident alien individual or a foreign corporation that is engaged in a trade or business within the United States is subject to U.S. federal income tax on income that is \"effectively connected\" with the conduct of such trade or business. The tax is imposed at graduated rates (for nonresident alien individuals) or at the flat corporate rate of 21% (for foreign corporations) on net ECI, in the same manner as such income would be taxed if earned by a U.S. person.
3525: 
3526: **Attribution Through Partnerships (Section 875(1)).** Section 875(1) provides that a non-U.S. person who is a member of a partnership that is engaged in a U.S. trade or business is itself treated as engaged in such trade or business. This attribution rule means that if the CV is treated as engaged in a U.S. trade or business --- whether by virtue of its own activities or the activities of its portfolio companies conducted through it --- Sovereign Capital would be treated as engaged in a U.S. trade or business and would be subject to U.S. federal income tax on its allocable share of the CV\'s ECI.
3527: 
3528: **FIRPTA (Section 897).** The Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act, codified principally in Section 897 of the Code, provides that gain or loss realized by a non-U.S. person on the disposition of a \"United States real property interest\" (\"USRPI\") is treated as ECI, regardless of whether the non-U.S. person is otherwise engaged in a U.S. trade or business. A USRPI includes an interest in a domestic corporation that is a \"United States real property holding corporation\" (\"USRPHC\") --- i.e., a corporation whose U.S. real property interests equal or exceed 50% of the sum of its U.S. real property interests, foreign real property interests, and other business assets used in a trade or business. While the three current portfolio companies (Luminos, ClearArc, and Vectral) are primarily software and technology companies, the determination of USRPHC status requires periodic analysis, and any significant real property holdings by these companies (including leasehold interests in certain circumstances) could trigger USRPI classification.
3529: 
3530: **Section 1446 Withholding.** Under Section 1446, a partnership that has income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business is required to withhold tax on the allocable share of such income attributable to its foreign partners. The withholding rate is 21% for corporate foreign partners and the highest applicable rate for non-corporate foreign partners. Without a blocker, the CV would be required to withhold on Sovereign Capital\'s allocable share of any ECI recognized by the partnership.
3531: 
3532: **Filing Obligations.** Absent a blocker structure, Sovereign Capital would be required to file a U.S. federal income tax return (Form 1120-F for a foreign corporation) reporting its allocable share of CV income, as well as potentially state income tax returns in each jurisdiction in which the CV is treated as doing business. The administrative burden and compliance costs associated with these filing obligations are significant and represent an independent reason for Sovereign Capital to invest through a blocker entity.
3533: 
3534: If Sovereign Capital (\$75 million) were to hold its CV interest directly, it would be exposed to: (i) U.S. federal income taxation on its allocable share of ECI at the 21% corporate rate; (ii) FIRPTA withholding under Section 1445 on dispositions of USRPIs; (iii) Section 1446 withholding on its allocable share of ECI; and (iv) U.S. federal and state income tax return filing obligations. The blocker structure recommended herein is designed to eliminate or mitigate each of these consequences.
3535: 
3536: **[IV. Proposed Domestic blocker Structure --- PCV Domestic blocker Inc.]{.underline}**
3537: 
3538: **[A. Entity Selection and Formation]{.underline}**
3539: 
3540: We recommend the formation of a single domestic blocker entity with the following characteristics:
3541: 
3542: > **Entity Name:** PCV Domestic blocker Inc.
3543: >
3544: > **Entity Type:** Delaware C-corporation
3545: >
3546: > **Jurisdiction of Formation:** State of Delaware
3547: >
3548: > **EIN:** To be applied for upon formation (Form SS-4 to be filed with the Internal Revenue Service)

These positions, which represent the highest-conviction, longest-duration assets in Fund II\'s portfolio, are as follows:

**Luminos Systems Inc.** Luminos Systems Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation (EIN: 47-8823156) engaged in the development and commercialization of enterprise-grade artificial intelligence and machine learning infrastructure software. As of June 30, 2025, the fair market value of Fund II\'s interest in Luminos is approximately \$612 million, against a cost basis of \$58.5 million, representing unrealized appreciation of \$553.5 million. Fund II holds approximately 24.7% of Luminos on a fully diluted basis. Luminos is headquartered in San Francisco, California.

**ClearArc Software Inc.** ClearArc Software Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation (EIN: 83-5519274) specializing in cybersecurity and data compliance solutions for regulated financial institutions. The fair market value of Fund II\'s interest in ClearArc as of June 30, 2025 is approximately \$468 million, against a cost basis of \$37.4 million, representing unrealized appreciation of \$430.6 million. Fund II holds approximately 31.2% of ClearArc on a fully diluted basis. ClearArc is headquartered in Austin, Texas.

**Vectral Cloud Inc.** Vectral Cloud Inc. is a Delaware C-corporation (EIN: 85-1102847) engaged in the provision of hybrid cloud infrastructure and edge computing services. The fair market value of Fund II\'s interest in Vectral as of June 30, 2025 is approximately \$260 million, against a cost basis of \$42.1 million, representing unrealized appreciation of \$217.9 million. Fund II holds approximately 18.9% of Vectral on a fully diluted basis. Vectral is headquartered in Denver, Colorado.

In the aggregate, the three portfolio company positions have a combined fair market value of \$1.34 billion and a combined cost basis of \$138 million, resulting in total unrealized built-in gain of \$1.202 billion. The implied gross multiple on invested capital (\"MOIC\") for the three positions is approximately 9.71×.

The transfer of the three portfolio company interests from Fund II to the CV will be structured as a contribution under Section 721 of the Code, which provides for non-recognition of gain or loss on contributions of property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. The Section 721 contribution will give rise to the Section 704(c) built-in gain allocations discussed in detail in Section VIII of this memorandum and in the companion Section 704(c) Allocation Methodology Memo.
**[B. CV Capitalization]{.underline}**
The CV will be capitalized from three sources:

**Rolling LPs.** Existing limited partners of Fund II who elect to roll their interests into the CV (rather than cash out) will contribute approximately \$680 million in NAV to the CV. These rolling LPs include, among others, Meridian Public Employees\' Retirement System, Ashford University Endowment, and Sovereign Capital Partners (Cayman) Ltd. --- the three investors who are the subjects of this memorandum --- as well as various other institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals who are not expected to require blocker structures.

**New Secondary Capital.** Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP, a secondary buyer vehicle managed by Garrison Capital Advisors LLC, will commit \$380 million of new capital as the lead secondary buyer in the transaction. Garrison\'s commitment represents the principal source of fresh capital for the CV. The primary contact at Garrison is Mitchell Adler, Partner. Garrison\'s outside legal counsel is Whitfield & Calloway LLP, with Douglas Whitfield, Partner, serving as lead outside counsel.
**GP Co-Investment.** Pinnacle Capital Management LLC and its principals will make a co-investment of \$14 million into the CV, consistent with standard general partner co-investment practices.

Total CV capitalization at close is projected to be \$1.074 billion. Of the \$380 million in Garrison secondary capital, approximately \$280 million will be used to provide liquidity to Fund II limited partners who elect to cash out of the continuation vehicle transaction. The remaining \$100 million will be designated for follow-on investment reserves and fund-level expenses.

The CV will be formed as a Delaware limited partnership, Pinnacle Continuation Vehicle LP, with a new general partner entity, Pinnacle CV Partners LLC, to be formed as a Delaware limited liability company. Hawthorne Reid LLP (Vanessa Liu, Partner) is serving as fund formation counsel and is responsible for preparing the limited partnership agreement and related formation documents.

The proposed economics of the CV are as follows: a management fee of 1.25% per annum calculated on net asset value; carried interest of 15% over a 7% annual preferred return calculated on a European-style (whole-fund) waterfall basis; and a fund term of five years from the date of the final close, subject to two one-year extension periods at the discretion of the general partner, in each case subject to the consent of the LP advisory committee.
**[C. Investors Requiring blocker Protection]{.underline}**

Three limited partners of Fund II, each of which is electing to roll 100% of its existing Fund II interests into the CV, have been identified as requiring blocker entity protection for U.S. federal income tax purposes. The relevant characteristics of each investor are summarized below.

**Meridian Public Employees\' Retirement System.** Meridian is a U.S. tax-exempt public pension fund qualifying for exemption from U.S. federal income tax under Sections 501(a) and 401(a) of the Code. Meridian\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$125 million, and it is electing a 100% rollover of its Fund II interest into the CV. The primary contact at Meridian is Trevor Huang, Chief Investment Officer. Meridian has expressed a high degree of sensitivity to any structural arrangement that could result in the recognition of UBTI, and its investment committee approval for participation in the CV is conditioned on the availability of UBTI-blocking protection.

**Ashford University Endowment.** Ashford is a U.S. tax-exempt educational endowment qualifying for exemption from U.S. federal income tax under Section 501(c)(3) of the Code. Ashford\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$50 million, and it is likewise electing a 100% rollover into the CV. The primary contact at Ashford is Camille Berger, Director of Investments. Like Meridian, Ashford has a high sensitivity to UBTI exposure and requires blocker protection as a condition of its continued participation.

**Sovereign Capital Partners (Cayman) Ltd.** Sovereign Capital is a Cayman Islands exempted company that serves as a non-U.S. feeder vehicle for a consortium of Asian family offices. Sovereign Capital\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$75 million, and it is electing a 100% rollover into the CV. The primary contact is Kenneth Fong, Managing Director. Sovereign Capital has expressed a high degree of sensitivity to exposure to U.S. effectively connected income, FIRPTA withholding, and the administrative burden of direct U.S. income tax return filing obligations.
**[III. The Need for blocker Structures]{.underline}**
**[A. UBTI Concerns for Tax-Exempt Investors]{.underline}**

Organizations that qualify for exemption from U.S. federal income tax under Section 501(a) of the Code --- including pension funds qualifying under Section 401(a) (such as Meridian) and educational and charitable organizations qualifying under Section 501(c)(3) (such as Ashford) --- are generally exempt from U.S. federal income tax on their investment income. This exemption, however, is subject to a significant exception: tax-exempt organizations are subject to tax on UBTI as defined in Section 512 of the Code.

UBTI is broadly defined to include gross income derived by an exempt organization from any unrelated trade or business regularly carried on by the organization, less the deductions directly connected with the carrying on of such trade or business. The UBTI rules are designed to prevent tax-exempt organizations from enjoying a competitive advantage over taxable enterprises by conducting commercial activities under the umbrella of their tax-exempt status.
Several features of the CV structure create potential UBTI exposure for Meridian and Ashford if they were to invest directly as limited partners in the CV:

**Debt-Financed Income (Section 512(b)(4)).** Under Section 512(b)(4) of the Code, income derived from debt-financed property is treated as UBTI to the extent that such property is financed with \"acquisition indebtedness\" as defined in Section 514. If the CV were to incur borrowings --- whether through a subscription-line credit facility, a leveraged co-investment alongside a portfolio company, or other forms of fund-level or investment-level indebtedness --- the income allocable to the debt-financed portion of the CV\'s investments would constitute UBTI to Meridian and Ashford. This risk is particularly acute in the present context because the CV\'s \$100 million follow-on reserve may be supplemented by borrowings to finance additional investments in the three portfolio companies, and the CV may also enter into a subscription credit facility to manage the timing of capital calls and distributions.

**Income from Partnership Interests (Section 512(c)).** Under Section 512(c), a tax-exempt organization that is a partner in a partnership is treated as having derived its allocable share of the partnership\'s gross income from an unrelated trade or business, to the extent the partnership itself is engaged in such a trade or business. While the CV\'s primary activity --- holding equity interests in portfolio companies structured as C-corporations --- does not itself constitute an unrelated trade or business, the CV\'s ancillary activities (such as providing management consulting services to portfolio companies, if applicable) could give rise to UBTI allocable to its partners.

**Interaction of UBTI and Partnership Allocations.** More generally, because the CV is structured as a pass-through entity for U.S. federal income tax purposes, any item of income, gain, deduction, or loss recognized at the partnership level flows through to the partners in accordance with their distributive shares under the limited partnership agreement. To the extent any such item constitutes UBTI, it retains that character in the hands of the tax-exempt partners. This includes not only operating income and debt-financed income, but also certain categories of fee income and other amounts that may be treated as UBTI under the broad definitional framework of Section 512.

If Meridian (\$125 million) and Ashford (\$50 million) were to hold their CV interests directly, they would be exposed to UBTI on: (i) debt-financed portfolio income to the extent the CV or any blocker-equivalent intermediate entity utilizes leverage, (ii) any operating income allocations from portfolio companies to the extent structured as pass-through entities (though the three current portfolio companies are C-corporations, there is no guarantee that the CV will not make follow-on investments in entities organized as partnerships or LLCs), and (iii) certain fee-related income. The magnitude of this exposure could be substantial, particularly if the CV utilizes leverage in connection with follow-on investments from the \$100 million reserve.
**[B. ECI and FIRPTA Concerns for Non-U.S. Investors]{.underline}**
Non-U.S. investors who hold interests in a U.S. partnership that is engaged in a U.S. trade or business face a distinct but equally significant set of adverse U.S. federal income tax consequences.

**Effectively Connected Income (Sections 871(b) and 882(a)).** Under Sections 871(b) and 882(a) of the Code, a nonresident alien individual or a foreign corporation that is engaged in a trade or business within the United States is subject to U.S. federal income tax on income that is \"effectively connected\" with the conduct of such trade or business. The tax is imposed at graduated rates (for nonresident alien individuals) or at the flat corporate rate of 21% (for foreign corporations) on net ECI, in the same manner as such income would be taxed if earned by a U.S. person.

**Attribution Through Partnerships (Section 875(1)).** Section 875(1) provides that a non-U.S. person who is a member of a partnership that is engaged in a U.S. trade or business is itself treated as engaged in such trade or business. This attribution rule means that if the CV is treated as engaged in a U.S. trade or business --- whether by virtue of its own activities or the activities of its portfolio companies conducted through it --- Sovereign Capital would be treated as engaged in a U.S. trade or business and would be subject to U.S. federal income tax on its allocable share of the CV\'s ECI.

**FIRPTA (Section 897).** The Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act, codified principally in Section 897 of the Code, provides that gain or loss realized by a non-U.S. person on the disposition of a \"United States real property interest\" (\"USRPI\") is treated as ECI, regardless of whether the non-U.S. person is otherwise engaged in a U.S. trade or business. A USRPI includes an interest in a domestic corporation that is a \"United States real property holding corporation\" (\"USRPHC\") --- i.e., a corporation whose U.S. real property interests equal or exceed 50% of the sum of its U.S. real property interests, foreign real property interests, and other business assets used in a trade or business. While the three current portfolio companies (Luminos, ClearArc, and Vectral) are primarily software and technology companies, the determination of USRPHC status requires periodic analysis, and any significant real property holdings by these companies (including leasehold interests in certain circumstances) could trigger USRPI classification.

**Section 1446 Withholding.** Under Section 1446, a partnership that has income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business is required to withhold tax on the allocable share of such income attributable to its foreign partners. The withholding rate is 21% for corporate foreign partners and the highest applicable rate for non-corporate foreign partners. Without a blocker, the CV would be required to withhold on Sovereign Capital\'s allocable share of any ECI recognized by the partnership.

**Filing Obligations.** Absent a blocker structure, Sovereign Capital would be required to file a U.S. federal income tax return (Form 1120-F for a foreign corporation) reporting its allocable share of CV income, as well as potentially state income tax returns in each jurisdiction in which the CV is treated as doing business. The administrative burden and compliance costs associated with these filing obligations are significant and represent an independent reason for Sovereign Capital to invest through a blocker entity.

If Sovereign Capital (\$75 million) were to hold its CV interest directly, it would be exposed to: (i) U.S. federal income taxation on its allocable share of ECI at the 21% corporate rate; (ii) FIRPTA withholding under Section 1445 on dispositions of USRPIs; (iii) Section 1446 withholding on its allocable share of ECI; and (iv) U.S. federal and state income tax return filing obligations. The blocker structure recommended herein is designed to eliminate or mitigate each of these consequences.
**[IV. Proposed Domestic blocker Structure --- PCV Domestic blocker Inc.]{.underline}**
**[A. Entity Selection and Formation]{.underline}**
We recommend the formation of a single domestic blocker entity with the following characteristics:
> **Entity Name:** PCV Domestic blocker Inc.
> **Entity Type:** Delaware C-corporation
> **Jurisdiction of Formation:** State of Delaware
> **EIN:** To be applied for upon formation (Form SS-4 to be filed with the Internal Revenue Service)

California does not conform to the federal Section 1202 QSBS exclusion. Revenue and Taxation Code Section 18152.5 expressly decouples California from Section 1202, effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2013. Accordingly, all gain on the ultimate disposition of the portfolio company shares will be subject to California income tax at ordinary income rates (currently up to 13.3%) for California-resident LPs and to the extent the income is characterized as California-source income.

Under Section 1061, if gain is allocated with respect to an API and the gain would otherwise be treated as long-term capital gain, the gain is recharacterized as short-term capital gain (taxed at ordinary income rates of up to 37% federal) unless the partnership\'s holding period in the underlying asset exceeds three years (rather than the standard one-year holding period for long-term capital gain treatment). This effectively imposes a three-year holding period on carried interest gains.

Fund II\'s carried interest is structured as a 20% carry over an 8% preferred return (compounded annually) with a 100% GP catch-up. The carried interest has been held by Pinnacle Capital Partners II LLC (Fund II\'s GP) and the GP principals since the fund\'s final close in December 2019. The Section 1061 three-year holding period was therefore satisfied as of December 2022. All gains currently allocated to the Fund II carried interest qualify for long-term capital gain treatment under Section 1061, provided that the underlying portfolio companies have been held by Fund II for more than three years (which is the case for all three portfolio companies --- the most recent investment, Vectral, was made in March 2021, more than four years ago).

**Result.** The legacy carry tranche in the CV will inherit the Fund II holding period. Because the Section 1061 three-year holding period was already satisfied as of December 2022, gains allocated to the legacy carry tranche should qualify for long-term capital gain treatment immediately upon CV closing. This is a significant benefit, as it avoids the three-year waiting period that would apply to newly issued carried interest.

In addition to the legacy carry tranche, the GP will be entitled to a new carried interest in the CV on the terms described in Section III.B (15% over 7% preferred return, European-style waterfall). This new carry constitutes a newly issued API with a holding period commencing at the CV closing (estimated October 31, 2025).

Each principal\'s API holding period is tracked independently. All three principals have held the Fund II carried interest since December 2019 and therefore have a legacy carry holding period of approximately five years and eight months as of the date of this memorandum. The new carry holding period for each principal will commence at the CV closing date.

Capital gains on the GP co-invest are subject to the standard one-year holding period for long-term capital gain treatment, not the Section 1061 three-year requirement. Under Section 1223(1), the GP\'s holding period in the co-invest will begin at the CV closing date (October 31, 2025), and the standard one-year holding period will be satisfied by November 2026.

The purpose of this memorandum is to recommend the optimal blocker entity architecture for the proposed Pinnacle Continuation Vehicle LP (\"PCV\" or the \"CV\") to accommodate two distinct categories of investors who require structural insulation from adverse U.S. federal income tax consequences arising from direct participation in a domestic limited partnership: (a) U.S. tax-exempt limited partners requiring protection from unrelated business taxable income (\"UBTI\") under Section 512 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the \"Code\"), and (b) non-U.S. limited partners requiring protection from effectively connected income (\"ECI\") and withholding obligations under the Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act of 1980 (\"FIRPTA\") as codified in Sections 897 and 1446 of the Code.

Both blocker entities should be formed by September 30, 2025, ahead of the target first close on October 15, 2025 and the anticipated final close on October 31, 2025. This timeline accommodates the filing of the Form 8832 check-the-box election for PCV International Holdings Ltd., which must be filed no later than 75 days after formation to be effective as of the date of formation, and allows adequate time for capitalization and subscription into the CV prior to the first close.

Fund II is a 2019 vintage fund. Its final close occurred in December 2019, with total committed capital of \$875 million. As of the date of this memorandum, called capital stands at approximately \$831.25 million, representing a 95% draw-down ratio. Based on the audited financials prepared by Andover & Strauss LLP as of June 30, 2025, Fund II\'s gross net asset value (\"NAV\") is approximately \$1.82 billion, and its net NAV (after deduction of accrued carried interest, management fees, and fund expenses) is approximately \$1.56 billion. Fund II has generated strong returns since inception, driven principally by the appreciation of its three largest portfolio company positions, which collectively represent the substantial majority of fund value.

The proposed economics of the CV are as follows: a management fee of 1.25% per annum calculated on net asset value; carried interest of 15% over a 7% annual preferred return calculated on a European-style (whole-fund) waterfall basis; and a fund term of five years from the date of the final close, subject to two one-year extension periods at the discretion of the general partner, in each case subject to the consent of the LP advisory committee.

**Sovereign Capital Partners (Cayman) Ltd.** Sovereign Capital is a Cayman Islands exempted company that serves as a non-U.S. feeder vehicle for a consortium of Asian family offices. Sovereign Capital\'s original commitment to Fund II was \$75 million, and it is electing a 100% rollover into the CV. The primary contact is Kenneth Fong, Managing Director. Sovereign Capital has expressed a high degree of sensitivity to exposure to U.S. effectively connected income, FIRPTA withholding, and the administrative burden of direct U.S. income tax return filing obligations.

UBTI is broadly defined to include gross income derived by an exempt organization from any unrelated trade or business regularly carried on by the organization, less the deductions directly connected with the carrying on of such trade or business. The UBTI rules are designed to prevent tax-exempt organizations from enjoying a competitive advantage over taxable enterprises by conducting commercial activities under the umbrella of their tax-exempt status.

**Effectively Connected Income (Sections 871(b) and 882(a)).** Under Sections 871(b) and 882(a) of the Code, a nonresident alien individual or a foreign corporation that is engaged in a trade or business within the United States is subject to U.S. federal income tax on income that is \"effectively connected\" with the conduct of such trade or business. The tax is imposed at graduated rates (for nonresident alien individuals) or at the flat corporate rate of 21% (for foreign corporations) on net ECI, in the same manner as such income would be taxed if earned by a U.S. person.

**Section 1446 Withholding.** Under Section 1446, a partnership that has income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business is required to withhold tax on the allocable share of such income attributable to its foreign partners. The withholding rate is 21% for corporate foreign partners and the highest applicable rate for non-corporate foreign partners. Without a blocker, the CV would be required to withhold on Sovereign Capital\'s allocable share of any ECI recognized by the partnership.

If Sovereign Capital (\$75 million) were to hold its CV interest directly, it would be exposed to: (i) U.S. federal income taxation on its allocable share of ECI at the 21% corporate rate; (ii) FIRPTA withholding under Section 1445 on dispositions of USRPIs; (iii) Section 1446 withholding on its allocable share of ECI; and (iv) U.S. federal and state income tax return filing obligations. The blocker structure recommended herein is designed to eliminate or mitigate each of these consequences.

This result follows from the operation of Section 512(b)(1) of the Code, which excludes from the computation of UBTI all dividends received by a tax-exempt organization. Because distributions from PCV Domestic blocker Inc. to Meridian and Ashford will take the form of dividends on corporate stock (or, in the case of a liquidating distribution, a return of capital and/or capital gain from the disposition of stock), such amounts are excluded from UBTI by statute. The interposition of the C-corporation blocker between the tax-exempt investors and the partnership effectively converts what would otherwise be items of UBTI (if received directly through the partnership) into dividend income, which is specifically excluded from the UBTI computation.
The Form 8832 election must be filed within the following timeframe to be effective as of the date of formation:
> • The election may specify an effective date that is no earlier than 75 days before the date the election is filed.
> • The election may specify an effective date that is no later than 12 months after the date the election is filed.

> • To ensure that the election is effective from the date of formation (anticipated to be September 30, 2025), the Form 8832 should be filed no later than December 14, 2025 (75 days after September 30, 2025).

**Branch Profits Tax (Section 884).** One significant additional tax cost associated with the Offshore blocker structure must be noted. Under Section 884 of the Code, a foreign corporation that has income effectively connected with a U.S. trade or business is subject to a \"branch profits tax\" on its \"dividend equivalent amount\" --- broadly, the effectively connected earnings and profits of the foreign corporation that are distributed or deemed distributed to its shareholders. The branch profits tax is imposed at a rate of 30%, in addition to the regular corporate income tax on ECI.

The branch profits tax rate may be reduced by an applicable U.S. income tax treaty between the United States and the country of which the foreign corporation is a resident. However, the Cayman Islands does not have an income tax treaty with the United States. Accordingly, PCV International Holdings Ltd. will be subject to the full 30% branch profits tax rate on its effectively connected earnings and profits that are distributed or deemed distributed to Sovereign Capital.

As discussed more fully in Section VIII below and in the companion Section 704(c) Allocation Methodology Memo, the recommended remedial allocation method under Section 704(c) is designed to allocate pre-contribution built-in gain to the contributing (rolling) partners, and not to new investors (such as Garrison Secondaries Fund IV LP) who are investing fresh capital in the CV. This is a critical distinction. Meridian, Ashford, and Sovereign Capital are all rolling their existing Fund II interests into the CV. Their pro-rata shares of the \$1.202 billion built-in gain will be allocated to them --- through the respective blocker entities --- under Section 704(c). In contrast, Garrison, as a new secondary buyer contributing fresh capital, will not bear any Section 704(c) built-in gain allocations.

In addition, PCV International Holdings Ltd. will be subject to the 30% branch profits tax on its effectively connected earnings and profits to the extent distributed or deemed distributed to Sovereign Capital. If the full after-tax earnings (\$132.6M − \$27.8M = \$104.8M) were repatriated, the branch profits tax would be approximately:

> *Option A:* Two directors designated by Meridian (as the majority shareholder) and one director designated by Ashford. This approach reflects the relative economic interests of the shareholders and gives Meridian, as the holder of approximately 71% of the equity, effective control of the board.

The draft Tax Protection Agreement for the CV --- currently being prepared under a separate workstream --- will provide rolling LPs with contractual protections against the early disposition of contributed assets. These protections are designed to prevent the CV\'s general partner from triggering the recognition of built-in gain on the contributed portfolio company interests sooner than necessary, thereby deferring the partners\' (and the blocker entities\') tax liabilities.

File IRS Form 8832 (Entity Classification Election) for PCV International Holdings Ltd. (effective date: date of formation)   By September 30, 2025              Calderwood & Harkness LLP (Garrett Simmons)

The target dates set forth above are aggressive but achievable, provided that all parties commence work promptly and coordinate effectively. The most time-critical item is the formation of PCV International Holdings Ltd. and the filing of the Form 8832 check-the-box election. As discussed in Section V.B, failure to timely file this election would render the Offshore blocker ineffective as a blocker for U.S. tax purposes. We recommend that the Calderwood & Harkness team prepare the Form 8832 in advance and file it immediately upon confirmation of the entity\'s formation date.

As discussed in Sections V.D and VI.B above, PCV International Holdings Ltd. will be subject to the 30% branch profits tax under Section 884 of the Code on its effectively connected earnings and profits that are distributed or deemed distributed to Sovereign Capital. Because the Cayman Islands does not have an income tax treaty with the United States, there is no treaty-based reduction in the branch profits tax rate.
> • Changes to the definition of UBTI or to the dividend exclusion under Section 512(b)(1) could alter the effectiveness of the Domestic blocker;
> • Changes to the FIRPTA rules, the ECI rules, or the branch profits tax rate could alter the effectiveness or cost of the Offshore blocker; and
> • **Section 871(b)** --- Taxation of nonresident alien individuals on effectively connected income
> • **Section 882(a)** --- Taxation of foreign corporations on effectively connected income
> • **Section 1446** --- Withholding tax on foreign partners\' share of effectively connected income

> 4\. **IRS Form 8832 (Entity Classification Election)** --- to be filed with the Internal Revenue Service to elect classification as a corporation for U.S. federal tax purposes; effective date to be the date of formation.

matches.line: **Re: Engagement of Calderwood & Harkness LLP --- Side Letter Agreements and Most Favored Nation Election Framework for Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP**

Calderwood & Harkness LLP (\"Calderwood & Harkness\" or the \"Firm\") is pleased to confirm its engagement by Pinnacle Venture Capital Management LLC, a Delaware limited liability company (the \"GP\"), in its capacity as the general partner of Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP, a Delaware limited partnership (the \"Fund\"), in connection with the negotiation, preparation, and documentation of side letter agreements with certain anchor limited partners of the Fund and the structuring and documentation of the most favored nation (\"MFN\") election framework applicable to qualifying limited partners of the Fund, each as more fully described in Section 2 below.

The Fund was organized pursuant to a Certificate of Limited Partnership filed with the Office of the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware on August 12, 2025, under File No. 7924813. The rights, obligations, and governance terms of the Fund and its limited partners will be set forth in the Amended and Restated Limited Partnership Agreement of the Fund, to be dated as of the date of the Fund\'s initial closing (the \"First Close\") (as may be further amended, restated, supplemented, or otherwise modified from time to time, the \"LPA\"). The side letters to be prepared in connection with this engagement will supplement and, solely as between the GP and the applicable limited partner, modify certain terms of the LPA in the manner described herein.
The scope of Calderwood & Harkness\'s engagement in connection with the Fund\'s side letter program and MFN election framework shall encompass the following:

Calderwood & Harkness will draft, negotiate, and finalize individual side letter agreements (each, a \"Side Letter\") with the following three anchor limited partners of the Fund (collectively, the \"Anchor LPs\"):

> \(i\) **Cascadia Public Employees\' Retirement System** (\"Cascadia PERS\"), a governmental pension plan organized under the laws of the State of Washington. Cascadia PERS has committed to a capital commitment to the Fund in the amount of Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$75,000,000), representing approximately 12.5% of the Fund\'s target fund size of Six Hundred Million Dollars (\$600,000,000) (the \"Target Fund Size\").

> \(ii\) **Northstar Endowment Partners LLC** (\"Northstar\"), a limited liability company organized under the laws of the State of Delaware, serving as the dedicated investment vehicle for the endowment of Veltrano University. Northstar has committed to a capital commitment to the Fund in the amount of Fifty Million Dollars (\$50,000,000), representing approximately 8.33% of the Target Fund Size.

> \(iii\) **Brindoval Family Office Holdings LP** (\"Brindoval\"), a limited partnership organized under the laws of the State of Delaware. Brindoval has committed to a capital commitment to the Fund in the amount of Forty Million Dollars (\$40,000,000), representing approximately 6.67% of the Target Fund Size.

The aggregate capital commitments of the Anchor LPs total One Hundred Sixty-Five Million Dollars (\$165,000,000), representing approximately 27.5% of the Target Fund Size. Given the significance of these commitments to the Fund\'s initial closing and overall capital formation, the Firm understands that the timely completion of Side Letter negotiations with each of the Anchor LPs is a priority for the GP.

Each Side Letter will be structured to supplement and, solely as between the GP and the applicable Anchor LP, modify certain terms and conditions of the LPA. The specific provisions to be addressed in each Side Letter will vary based on the nature, regulatory status, and specific requirements of the applicable Anchor LP, but are expected to include, as applicable, the following categories of terms:

> \(ii\) **Co-investment rights**, including rights to participate in co-investment opportunities alongside the Fund, allocation priority, notification procedures, and minimum co-investment allocation amounts;

> \(iii\) **Excuse and opt-out rights**, including the right of certain limited partners to be excused from, or to opt out of, specific Fund investments on the basis of legal, regulatory, tax, or policy considerations applicable to such limited partner;

> \(v\) **FOIA and public records protections**, particularly relevant to Cascadia PERS, including provisions addressing the treatment of Fund information in the event of a public records request, prior notice and consultation obligations of the limited partner, and the GP\'s right to seek protective relief;
> \(vi\) **Advisory committee seats**, including the right of certain Anchor LPs to designate a representative to serve on the Fund\'s advisory committee, as well as related governance provisions;

> \(vii\) **Key-person event notifications**, including enhanced notification rights in the event of a key-person event under the LPA, consultation rights, and accelerated information delivery timelines;

> \(viii\) **Transfer rights**, including any enhanced or modified transfer, assignment, or secondary sale rights negotiated with an Anchor LP, subject to the transfer restrictions and consent provisions of the LPA;

> \(ix\) **Fee netting provisions**, addressing the application and allocation of transaction fees, monitoring fees, break-up fees, and other fees received by the GP or its affiliates in connection with Fund investments;

> \(x\) **Information rights**, including the right to receive additional information from the GP regarding the Fund\'s investments, operations, or financial condition, beyond the standard reporting obligations set forth in the LPA; and

Calderwood & Harkness will structure and document a comprehensive most favored nation election framework (the \"MFN Framework\") applicable to qualifying limited partners of the Fund. The MFN Framework will include the following components:

> \(i\) **MFN Eligibility Threshold.** The Firm will advise on and document the MFN eligibility threshold, which the GP has preliminarily determined shall be set at capital commitments of Twenty-Five Million Dollars (\$25,000,000) or greater. Limited partners whose capital commitments equal or exceed this threshold (each, an \"Eligible LP\") will be entitled to elect certain rights and benefits granted in Side Letters to other limited partners of the Fund, subject to the exclusions described below.

> \(ii\) **MFN Election Procedures Letter and Election Form.** The Firm will draft a template MFN election procedures letter (the \"MFN Procedures Letter\") to be delivered by the GP to each Eligible LP, together with a standardized MFN election form (the \"MFN Election Form\") to be completed and returned by any Eligible LP wishing to make an MFN election. The purpose of this memorandum is to analyze the structuring of the most favored nation (\"MFN\") election framework and to develop a comprehensive, LP-by-LP negotiation strategy for the three anchor investor side letters in connection with Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP (the \"Fund\"), a Delaware limited partnership managed by its general partner, Pinnacle Venture Capital Management LLC (the \"GP\"). This memorandum is prepared to inform internal strategy discussions and to guide the drafting and negotiation of the side letter agreements anticipated to be delivered to counterparty counsel on or about October 20, 2025.

The Fund is targeting an aggregate capital raise of \$600,000,000 (with a hard cap of \$750,000,000) and will focus on early-stage and growth-stage venture capital investments in the enterprise software and software-as-a-service (\"SaaS\") sectors. The GP\'s principals, Rajesh Mehta and Claire Dubois, have established a strong track record through Pinnacle Venture Fund I LP (2021 vintage, \$350 million), which has generated a net internal rate of return (\"IRR\") of 24.3% and a net total value to paid-in multiple (\"TVPI\") of 1.58x as of June 30, 2025. The successor fund is well-positioned in the market, and the GP has attracted significant interest from institutional limited partners seeking exposure to the enterprise software sector.

Each of these anchor investors will execute a separate side letter agreement that supplements the Amended and Restated Limited Partnership Agreement of Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP (the \"LPA\"), which is expected to be dated as of the First Close on January 15, 2026. The side letters will grant various economic, governance, informational, and operational accommodations tailored to the legal status, investment policy requirements, and negotiating priorities of each anchor LP.

The key timeline milestones are as follows: initial drafts of the three anchor side letters are targeted for distribution to counterparty counsel by October 20, 2025; the negotiation period is expected to extend through December 20, 2025 (with two to three rounds of mark-ups anticipated per side letter); the First Close is targeted for January 15, 2026; and the Final Close deadline is July 15, 2026. The MFN Side Letter Compilation will be delivered to all MFN-eligible limited partners within fifteen (15) business days following the Final Close.

Our central recommendation is to structure the MFN framework with robust \"Excluded Provisions\" carve-outs designed to limit the GP\'s economic and operational exposure from subsequent LP elections, while providing sufficient MFN coverage to satisfy the institutional expectations of sophisticated anchor investors. Specifically, we recommend defining five categories of Excluded Provisions (governmental plan regulatory requirements, ERISA representations, advisory committee seats, portfolio company board observer rights, and a catch-all for LP-specific legal/regulatory/tax provisions) while permitting MFN elections for economic terms (management fee reductions, co-investment terms, fee netting) and information/notification rights.

The most favored nation clause is a standard feature in institutional fund side letters, particularly for anchor and early-closing investors. The MFN clause provides qualifying limited partners with the right to elect into more favorable terms that may be granted to other investors in the Fund, whether at the same closing or at subsequent closings. The purpose of the MFN clause is to protect early investors from economic disadvantage relative to later investors who may negotiate more favorable terms, and to provide a mechanism for equalizing the treatment of similarly situated limited partners.

The MFN framework will be implemented as follows: each anchor side letter will include an MFN election right provision, and the same provision (or a substantively identical provision) will be included in the side letters of all subsequent LPs whose commitments meet or exceed the MFN eligibility threshold. Separately, the GP will prepare a template MFN Election Procedures Letter and MFN Election Form, which will be distributed as part of the side letter package following the Final Close. All side letters, the LPA, and the MFN framework documents will be governed by the laws of the State of Delaware.

We recommend establishing the MFN eligibility threshold at a commitment amount of \$25,000,000 or greater to the Fund. Only limited partners whose aggregate capital commitments (including any commitments made at subsequent closings) equal or exceed \$25,000,000 will be entitled to exercise MFN election rights.

> • **GP expectations regarding LP base.** The GP has indicated that it expects the Fund\'s LP base to consist of approximately twenty to twenty-five limited partners, with the majority committing \$25,000,000 or more. The \$25M threshold thus captures the core institutional LP base while excluding a small number of smaller investors who may be admitted at later closings.
