**Amendment of electing LP\'s side letter.** Upon the GP\'s receipt of a valid and timely MFN Election Form, the electing LP\'s side letter is deemed automatically amended to incorporate the elected provisions, as though such provisions had been included in the electing LP\'s side letter as of its original execution date. No separate amendment agreement is required, although the GP may, at its discretion, prepare and circulate a confirmation letter reflecting the amended terms.

**GP discretion regarding applicability.** The GP retains discretion to determine whether a particular provision is \"applicable\" to the electing LP. This discretion is intended to address situations in which an MFN-eligible provision is, as drafted, specific to the legal, regulatory, or tax status of the LP to whom it was originally granted and would be inapplicable or meaningless if adopted by the electing LP. For example, a provision granting a fee reduction that is expressly conditioned on the LP\'s status as a tax-exempt organization may not be applicable to a taxable LP. The GP\'s determination of applicability must be made in good faith and on a reasonable basis. We anticipate that this discretion will be a point of negotiation with counterparty counsel, and we should be prepared to provide examples of circumstances in which the GP\'s discretion would appropriately be exercised.

**Preservation of LP confidentiality.** There is no requirement for the GP to notify the limited partner whose term was elected into by another LP. The confidentiality of each LP\'s identity and the specific terms of its side letter are preserved throughout the MFN process. The MFN Side Letter Compilation itself is delivered on a confidential basis and is subject to the confidentiality provisions of the LPA.

The first category of Excluded Provisions covers any provision that is included in a side letter to satisfy the specific legal or regulatory requirements of a limited partner that is a governmental pension plan, governmental retirement system, or sovereign entity. This category is designed to capture provisions that are legally mandated for governmental investors and that have no economic value, relevance, or applicability to non-governmental limited partners.

The primary beneficiary of this exclusion is Cascadia Public Employees\' Retirement System, which is a Washington State governmental pension plan that is tax-exempt under Internal Revenue Code Section 115. As a governmental entity, CPERS is subject to Washington State public records laws (the Washington Public Records Act, RCW 42.56), sunshine law requirements, and state-law mandated investment restrictions that do not apply to private institutional investors, endowments, or family offices. The side letter provisions granted to CPERS to address these requirements --- including FOIA/public records protections, notice and consultation rights before disclosure of Fund information in response to public records requests, and redaction procedures for proprietary Fund information --- are driven entirely by CPERS\'s governmental status and are not economic accommodations subject to competitive equalization through MFN elections.

The second category of Excluded Provisions covers representations that a limited partner is not subject to the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, as amended (\"ERISA\"), or waivers of ERISA-related representations that may be included in the LPA.

The primary beneficiary of this exclusion is Northstar Endowment Partners LLC, which is an investment vehicle for the endowment of Veltrano University. As a university endowment, NEP is not an \"employee benefit plan\" within the meaning of ERISA Section 3(3), and is not subject to the fiduciary duty, prohibited transaction, or plan asset rules of ERISA. NEP\'s side letter will include a representation that it is not a \"benefit plan investor\" (as defined in 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-101) and a waiver of any ERISA-related representations that may be included in the LPA.
The third category of Excluded Provisions covers the right to designate a representative to the Fund\'s advisory committee (also referred to as the LP Advisory Committee or \"LPAC\").

The primary beneficiary of this exclusion is Northstar Endowment Partners LLC, which has been granted a seat on the Fund\'s advisory committee through its side letter. We note, however, that CPERS is separately entitled to an advisory committee seat under the LPA itself, as a limited partner with a commitment of \$50,000,000 or more. CPERS\'s advisory committee entitlement does not arise from the side letter and therefore does not create MFN exposure; however, this distinction should be noted clearly in the CPERS side letter to avoid any ambiguity.

The rationale for this exclusion is grounded in the GP\'s governance prerogatives. Advisory committee composition is determined by the GP based on a range of considerations, including the mix of LP types (pension funds, endowments, family offices), commitment sizes, industry expertise, geographic diversity, and overall governance needs. The advisory committee serves important functions, including reviewing and approving conflicts of interest, reviewing valuations, and providing input on key fund decisions. The GP must retain discretion over the size and composition of the committee, and allowing MFN elections into advisory committee seats would undermine that discretion by creating an open-ended entitlement for any MFN-eligible LP to claim a seat.

Market practice strongly supports the exclusion of advisory committee seats from MFN. In our experience, virtually all institutional fund side letters treat advisory committee designations as excluded from MFN, and this position is generally accepted by institutional LPs and their counsel without significant pushback. We do not anticipate that this category will be a point of contention in the negotiations.
The fourth category of Excluded Provisions covers rights to designate a non-voting observer to the board of directors of one or more portfolio companies of the Fund.

The rationale for this exclusion is that board observer seats are inherently limited in number, are subject to portfolio company consent, and carry significant governance and confidentiality implications. Portfolio companies --- particularly early-stage and growth-stage companies --- may object to the appointment of multiple board observers, and the GP\'s ability to grant observer seats is constrained by the terms of its investment agreements with portfolio companies. Allowing MFN elections into board observer rights could result in an unmanageable number of observer designations, creating practical and legal complications at the portfolio company level.
This is a forward-looking exclusion designed to protect the GP\'s flexibility, and we do not anticipate that it will be a point of negotiation with the anchor LPs or their counsel.

**Basis for Exclusion.** CPERS is a governmental plan as defined in Section 414(d) of the Internal Revenue Code, exempt from federal income taxation under IRC § 115. CPERS\'s investment in the Fund imposes a range of regulatory and administrative burdens on the GP that are unique to governmental plan investors, including:

> • Compliance with state freedom of information and public records laws, which require the GP to cooperate with CPERS\'s disclosure obligations and may result in disclosure of Fund information that would otherwise be confidential;

> • Enhanced reporting requirements, including sector-level attribution and disaggregated performance data, that exceed the standard reporting obligations under the LPA and impose additional administrative costs on the GP and its fund administrator; and

**Delaware Fund Practice.** There is precedent in Delaware fund side letter practice for GPs to exclude fee concessions granted to governmental plans from MFN eligibility by characterizing them as linked to the regulatory burdens associated with governmental plan investments. The argument is that the fee reduction is not a standalone commercial concession but rather an integral component of a package of provisions that, taken together, address the specific legal, regulatory, and administrative requirements of the governmental plan LP. Under this characterization, the fee reduction is inseparable from the FOIA carve-outs, excuse rights, and enhanced reporting requirements granted to CPERS, and the entire package constitutes Excluded Provisions under Category 1 or Category 4 of the MFN framework.

An alternative approach --- and potentially the most effective structural solution --- would be to restructure the management fee concessions as commitment-based tiers in the LPA itself, rather than granting ad hoc fee reductions in individual side letters. Under this approach, the LPA would establish a tiered fee schedule in which the management fee rate decreases as a function of commitment size:

Under this structure, CPERS (at \$75,000,000) would receive the 1.75% rate as a function of the LPA\'s tiered fee schedule, not as a side letter concession. Similarly, NEP (at \$50,000,000) would receive the 1.85% rate based on its commitment level. Brindoval (at \$40,000,000) would remain at the standard 2.00% rate, consistent with its current terms.

**MFN Implications.** Commitment-based fee tiers established in the LPA are structural terms available to all limited partners at the corresponding commitment level. They are not side letter concessions and are therefore not subject to MFN election. An LP committing \$30,000,000 would not be able to elect into the 1.75% or 1.85% rate through the MFN process, because those rates are LPA-level terms conditioned on commitment thresholds, not side letter provisions that can be adopted regardless of commitment size.
> \(a\) It eliminates MFN fee exposure entirely with respect to the tiered rates, because the fee concessions are embedded in the LPA rather than in side letters.

**Limitations.** The LPA\'s fee structure would need to be finalized before or at the First Close on January 15, 2026. This requires coordination with Rajesh Mehta and Claire Dubois to determine whether commitment-based fee tiers are commercially acceptable and whether the proposed tier breakpoints and rates are consistent with the GP\'s fundraising strategy. Additionally, the tier structure would need to be disclosed to all prospective limited partners during the fundraise, which could affect commitment dynamics --- some LPs might increase their commitments to reach a lower fee tier, while others might view the tiered structure as evidence that fee negotiation is possible and seek additional concessions.

**Example.** If the CPERS 1.75% fee reduction remains an MFN-eligible provision (because the exclusion argument in Section V.A.1 is not pursued or is not accepted), the MFN framework would provide that any subsequent LP electing the 1.75% rate must have committed at least \$75,000,000 to the Fund, matching CPERS\'s commitment level. Similarly, any LP electing the 1.85% Northstar rate would need to have committed at least \$50,000,000.

We note that commitment-matching conditions are not universally accepted in the market, and some LP counsel may resist them as inconsistent with the purpose of MFN provisions. However, they are not uncommon in larger funds and are generally defensible as a reasonable mechanism to ensure that fee concessions are commensurate with the commitment levels that justified them. We recommend discussing with Rajesh Mehta and Claire Dubois whether this approach is commercially acceptable in the context of the Fund\'s fundraise.

We recommend drafting the MFN clause to limit electable provisions to those that are \"more favorable\" *in context* --- specifically, the GP may require that an LP electing a provision must accept the full package of provisions (including any corresponding obligations, restrictions, or conditions) granted to the LP from whose side letter the provision is being elected, rather than cherry-picking individual provisions.

The Fund\'s MFN framework operates within the well-established Delaware fund side letter practice, which generally treats management fee concessions as MFN-eligible unless specifically excluded. Delaware limited partnership law affords broad freedom of contract, and the scope of MFN election rights is governed by the specific language of the LPA and the relevant side letters, not by statute or common law. There is no Delaware Chancery Court case law directly addressing the enforceability or scope of MFN election provisions in the fund context, though the Court of Chancery\'s emphasis on the primacy of contractual language in the limited partnership context (*see, e.g., Dieckman v. Regency GP LP*, 155 A.3d 358 (Del. 2017)) reinforces the importance of precise drafting.

The ILPA Principles, which are referenced by Brindoval\'s information rights request and are increasingly influential in the institutional LP community, support broad MFN transparency. The ILPA Reporting Template and accompanying guidance recommend that GPs provide full disclosure of side letter terms to all limited partners and afford subsequent investors the opportunity to elect the most favorable terms offered to any other investor. While the ILPA Principles are not legally binding, they reflect the expectations of a significant segment of the institutional LP market and inform the negotiating posture of many LP counsel.

The current market trend is toward increasing LP sophistication and counsel aggressiveness in the negotiation of MFN provisions. All three of the Fund\'s anchor LPs are represented by experienced fund formation counsel --- Whitfield & Gage LLP (for CPERS), Hollander McKee & Stone LLP (for NEP), and Prescott & Langley LLP (for Brindoval) --- each of which has a well-established practice of negotiating broad MFN rights for its clients. The subsequent LP base is likely to include investors represented by similarly experienced counsel, creating sustained pressure on the GP to maintain a broad and transparent MFN framework.

> 1\. **Excluded Provision Structuring.** Discuss with Nicholas Stern the approach to characterizing the CPERS management fee reduction as an Excluded Provision, and present the recommended implementation steps (including specific side letter language and MFN procedures letter drafting) to Rajesh Mehta and Claire Dubois for commercial input. This discussion should occur before the CPERS side letter is finalized, and ideally before any further anchor side letter revisions are circulated to LP counsel.

> 2\. **Commitment-Based Fee Tiers.** Evaluate the feasibility of converting fee concessions from ad hoc side letter provisions to LPA-level commitment-based tiers before the First Close on January 15, 2026. This approach requires amendment of the LPA\'s fee provisions and must be coordinated with Rajesh Mehta and Claire Dubois, as it affects the Fund\'s marketing and fundraising strategy. If the tier approach is adopted, the CPERS and NEP side letters will need to be revised to remove the fee concession provisions and instead reference the LPA fee schedule.

> 4\. **Fund Administrator Coordination.** Coordinate with Patricia Lam at Meridian Fund Services LLC to prepare fee modeling scenarios based on the three scenarios analyzed in this memorandum, updated as actual commitments crystallize during the fundraise. Meridian should be prepared to calculate and implement retroactive fee adjustments following the close of the MFN election period.

> 6\. **Co-Investment Fee/Carry Waiver.** Flag the CPERS no-management-fee, no-carried-interest co-investment provision as an additional source of MFN-eligible economic exposure that warrants further analysis. If significant co-investment activity is anticipated during the Fund\'s investment period, the economic impact of MFN elections on co-investment economics could be material and should be quantified in a supplemental memorandum.

This memorandum is intended solely for the use of the individuals to whom it is addressed and should not be disclosed to, or relied upon by, any third party without the prior written consent of Calderwood & Harkness LLP.*

matches.line: > **Re:** Engagement of Calderwood & Harkness LLP --- Structuring, Formation, and Fund-Raising for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP

Calderwood & Harkness LLP is pleased to confirm its engagement by Cobalt Ventures LP to serve as fund counsel in connection with the structuring, formation, and fund-raising for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP (the \"Fund\" or \"CLSO Fund I\"), a proposed Delaware limited partnership. We understand that the Fund will be Cobalt\'s inaugural dedicated opportunistic life-sciences investment vehicle, and that Cobalt is targeting aggregate committed capital of Seven Hundred Fifty Million Dollars (\$750,000,000), with a hard cap of One Billion Dollars (\$1,000,000,000).

By way of background, Cobalt is a California-headquartered venture capital sponsor focused on the biotechnology and life-sciences sectors. Founded in 2018 by Dr. Marcus Yeung and Priya Dasgupta, Cobalt currently manages approximately \$420 million in assets under management across two prior vintage vehicles --- Cobalt Ventures Fund A, LP (vintage 2019) and Cobalt Ventures Fund B, LP (vintage 2022). The launch of CLSO Fund I represents a significant strategic milestone for the Cobalt platform, expanding the firm\'s investment mandate into opportunistic life-sciences investments across stage, geography, and modality.

This Letter sets forth the terms under which Calderwood & Harkness will provide legal services in connection with the structuring, formation, and fund-raising of the Fund and related entities, and it supersedes any prior oral or written understandings between the parties regarding the scope and terms of this engagement.
In addition to Cobalt Ventures LP, Calderwood & Harkness\'s representation under this engagement extends to the following entities, each of which is to be formed in connection with the Fund:
> \(a\) **Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP** --- a Delaware limited partnership, to be formed, which will serve as the main investment vehicle for the Fund;
> \(b\) **Cobalt Life Sciences GP I, LLC** --- a Delaware limited liability company, to be formed, which will serve as the general partner of the Fund;

> \(c\) **Cobalt Life Sciences Management I, LLC** --- a Delaware limited liability company, to be formed, which will serve as the management company and will be party to the management agreement with the Fund; and

> \(d\) **Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I (Blocker), Inc.** --- a Delaware C-Corporation, to be formed if and when determined to be necessary or advisable for purposes of establishing a taxable blocker structure for certain categories of investors, including tax-exempt and non-U.S. limited partners.

The foregoing entities are collectively referred to herein as the \"Fund Entities.\" As formation documents are prepared and filed for each Fund Entity, such entity shall be deemed a client of the Firm under the terms of this Letter without the need for a separate engagement letter, unless the Firm and the Client agree otherwise in writing.

**Important Clarification Regarding Scope of Representation.** Calderwood & Harkness does not represent, and will not represent in connection with this engagement, any individual limited partner or prospective limited partner of the Fund, any placement agent engaged by the Fund (including sagebrush Capital Partners LLC), or any other third-party service provider to the Fund. Each such party should retain and rely upon its own independent legal counsel with respect to its interests in or obligations to the Fund.
**3.1 Fund Structuring and Entity Formation**

Calderwood & Harkness will advise the Client on the optimal legal and organizational structure for the Fund and will be responsible for the formation of each Fund Entity. This workstream will include the following:

> \(b\) **Fund Structuring Memorandum.** Preparation and delivery of a comprehensive Fund Structuring Memorandum setting forth Calderwood & Harkness\'s analysis and recommendations regarding the recommended fund architecture, including a diagram of the proposed entity structure, a summary of the principal advantages and disadvantages of each structural alternative considered, and our recommended approach. The target delivery date for the Fund Structuring Memorandum is **April 30, 2026**.

> \(c\) **Delaware Formation Filings.** Preparation and filing of the Certificate of Limited Partnership for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP, and the Certificates of Formation for Cobalt Life Sciences GP I, LLC and Cobalt Life Sciences Management I, LLC, with the Delaware Division of Corporations. If the blocker corporation is determined to be necessary, Calderwood & Harkness will also prepare and file the Certificate of Incorporation for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I (Blocker), Inc.
> \(d\) **EIN Applications.** Preparation and submission of IRS Form SS-4 (Application for Employer Identification Number) for CLSO Fund I, CLSO GP I, and CLSO Management I.

> \(e\) **Registered Agent Coordination.** Coordination with Hollowell Technologies, the Client\'s designated registered agent in Delaware, to ensure that each Fund Entity is properly set up for service of process and annual compliance filings.
Calderwood & Harkness will provide tax structuring advice in connection with the formation and operation of the Fund, including the following:

> \(a\) **Tax Structuring Memorandum.** Preparation and delivery of a Tax Structuring Memorandum addressing the following topics, among others: (i) unrelated business taxable income (\"UBTI\") and effectively connected income (\"ECI\") planning for tax-exempt and non-U.S. investors; (ii) the application of IRC §1061 to carried interest allocations, including holding period analysis and the implications of the three-year holding period requirement; (iii) state income tax nexus considerations for the Fund, the general partner, and the management company, with a particular focus on Delaware, California, Oregon, Connecticut, and Massachusetts; (iv) blocker corporation structuring, including the use of a Delaware C-Corporation to mitigate UBTI and ECI for certain categories of investors; and (v) carry escrow implications, including the tax treatment of amounts held in escrow and the timing of income recognition. The target delivery date for the Tax Structuring Memorandum is **April 30, 2026**.

> \(b\) **Coordination with Tax Advisor.** Calderwood & Harkness will coordinate with Greystone Tax Advisors LLC (Kenneth Liu, Managing Director), the Client\'s independent tax advisor, on all tax structuring matters. We understand that Greystone will be responsible for the preparation of the Fund\'s annual tax returns (Forms 1065 and Schedules K-1) and for providing ongoing tax compliance advice, and that Calderwood & Harkness\'s role is limited to tax structuring and tax-related provisions of the fund documents.
**3.3 Fund Documentation Drafting**
Calderwood & Harkness will prepare the principal fund documents for the Fund, including the following:

> \(a\) **Agreement of Limited Partnership.** Drafting of the Agreement of Limited Partnership of Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP (the \"LPA\"), including all schedules and exhibits thereto. The first draft of the LPA is targeted for delivery on or about **May 31, 2026**. The LPA will address, among other things, the following key economic and governance terms:
> • Carry Escrow: 30% of carried interest distributions to be held in escrow pending final liquidation of the Fund to secure the general partner\'s clawback obligation;

> • Clawback: Standard general partner clawback obligation, net of taxes, to be triggered upon final liquidation of the Fund to the extent the general partner has received carried interest distributions in excess of amounts to which it is entitled on a cumulative basis;
> • Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\") provisions, including composition, authority, and procedures for the resolution of conflicts of interest;

> • ERISA compliance provisions, including the Fund\'s election to qualify as a \"venture capital operating company\" (\"VCOC\") under Department of Labor Regulation §2510.3-101(d), and the related covenants and operating requirements necessary to maintain VCOC status.

> \(d\) **Subscription Agreement and Investor Questionnaire.** Preparation of the form Subscription Agreement and Investor Questionnaire to be executed by each limited partner at the time of its commitment to the Fund, including representations and warranties regarding accredited investor and qualified purchaser status, ERISA status, tax status, OFAC compliance, and beneficial ownership.

Calderwood & Harkness will prepare the confidential Private Placement Memorandum (the \"PPM\") for the Fund. The PPM will be the principal marketing and disclosure document used in connection with the offering of limited partnership interests in the Fund to prospective investors. We anticipate delivering an outline and first draft of the PPM on or about **June 30, 2026**. The PPM will include, among other things, the following:
> \(b\) A description of the Fund\'s investment strategy, investment process, and target sectors within the life-sciences space;
> \(c\) A comprehensive discussion of risk factors associated with an investment in the Fund, including market risks, strategy-specific risks, regulatory risks, and structural risks;

> \(f\) A summary of the material U.S. federal income tax considerations applicable to an investment in the Fund, including considerations for taxable U.S. investors, tax-exempt U.S. investors, and non-U.S. investors; and

Investment opportunities that fall outside the Partnership\'s stated investment strategy may be allocated to other Cobalt vehicles or investment activities. The General Partner shall maintain and apply a written investment allocation policy, which shall be available for review by the LPAC upon request.

\(c\) **Conflict Disclosure.** Conflicts of interest arising from co-investments, cross-transactions, allocation of investment opportunities, or transactions between the Partnership and Affiliates of the General Partner shall be disclosed to the LPAC. Any transaction between the Partnership and the General Partner or its Affiliates (other than as contemplated by this Agreement) shall require the prior approval of the LPAC.

\(a\) **Automatic Suspension.** Upon the occurrence of a Key Person Event, the Investment Period shall be automatically suspended, effective as of the date on which the Key Person Event occurs. The General Partner shall promptly notify all Limited Partners and the LPAC of the occurrence of a Key Person Event.
> \(ii\) Follow-on investments in existing Portfolio Companies shall be permitted only with the prior written consent of the LPAC;
> \(iii\) Capital calls shall be limited to amounts necessary to fund Fund Expenses, satisfy existing commitments and obligations of the Partnership, and pay Management Fees; and

> \(i\) A vote of the LPAC to reinstate the Investment Period, which vote may be taken upon (A) the cure of the Key Person Event (i.e., the return of the affected Key Person to full-time service) or (B) the identification and approval of a replacement Key Person pursuant to Section 10.4; or

\(d\) **Permanent Termination.** If the Investment Period is permanently terminated pursuant to clause (c)(ii) above, the Partnership shall enter its harvest period, during which the General Partner shall focus exclusively on the management, monitoring, and orderly realization of existing Portfolio Investments. No new investments or follow-on investments (except protective investments with LPAC consent) shall be made during the harvest period.

The General Partner may propose a replacement Key Person to the LPAC at any time following the occurrence of a Key Person Event. Reinstatement of the Investment Period following the identification of a replacement Key Person shall require the prior written approval of the LPAC. The LPAC shall consider, among other factors, the qualifications, experience, and track record of the proposed replacement Key Person in evaluating any such proposal.

\(a\) **General Restriction.** No Limited Partner may, directly or indirectly, sell, transfer, assign, pledge, hypothecate, encumber, or otherwise dispose of all or any portion of its Partnership Interest (a \"Transfer\"), without the prior written consent of the General Partner, which consent may be granted or withheld in the General Partner\'s sole and absolute discretion.
> \(iii\) Transfers to which the General Partner has provided its prior written consent.

> \(ii\) The transferee has executed such documents and instruments as the General Partner may reasonably require, including a joinder agreement and an assumption of the transferor\'s obligations under this Agreement;

\(a\) The General Partner may not Transfer its general partner interest in the Partnership without the prior written consent of Limited Partners holding a majority of the aggregate Capital Commitments (excluding the GP Commitment).

\(b\) Notwithstanding the foregoing, the General Partner may effect internal restructurings among the members of the General Partner (including admissions, withdrawals, and reallocations of economic interests among GP members) without Limited Partner consent, provided that such restructuring does not result in a change in the control or management of the General Partner or the Partnership.

No transferee of a Partnership Interest shall be admitted as a substituted Limited Partner of the Partnership unless (a) the General Partner has consented to such admission in writing, (b) the transferee has executed a joinder agreement and such other documents as the General Partner may require, and (c) all conditions to Transfer set forth in Section 11.1(c) have been satisfied. Until admitted as a substituted Limited Partner, a transferee shall have only the rights of an assignee under the DRULPA (i.e., the right to receive allocations and distributions, but no voting, consent, or other rights under this Agreement).

\(c\) **Fund Administration.** Fund administration, accounting, and NAV calculations shall be performed by Halcyon Fund Services, Inc. or such other fund administrator as the General Partner may engage from time to time.

\(c\) **Determination.** The General Partner shall determine in good faith whether the requested excuse is warranted. In the event of a dispute regarding the propriety of an excuse request, the General Partner shall consult with the LPAC before making a final determination. The General Partner\'s determination shall be final and binding on the requesting Limited Partner.
**[ARTICLE XIV --- LIMITED PARTNER ADVISORY COMMITTEE (LPAC)]{.underline}**

\(a\) **Establishment.** The General Partner shall establish a Limited Partner Advisory Committee (the \"LPAC\") promptly following the First Close. The LPAC shall consist of a minimum of three (3) and a maximum of seven (7) members.

\(b\) **Appointment.** Members of the LPAC shall be appointed by the General Partner from among the largest Limited Partners (measured by Capital Commitment). The General Partner shall endeavor to include at least one representative of a non-U.S. Limited Partner on the LPAC if non-U.S. Capital Commitments aggregate \$50,000,000 or more.

\(c\) **Initial LPAC.** The General Partner anticipates inviting representatives of the following entities to serve as initial LPAC members (subject to their admission as Limited Partners at the First Close): Ironwood PERS, Northgate Endowment Management LLC, and Pinnacle Insurance Group, Inc. Additional LPAC members may be appointed following the Final Close in accordance with this Section 14.1. The initial composition of the LPAC is set forth in Schedule E attached hereto.

\(d\) **Term and Removal.** Each LPAC member shall serve until the earlier of (i) such member\'s resignation from the LPAC, (ii) such member ceasing to hold a Partnership Interest, or (iii) removal by the General Partner for reasonable cause. The General Partner may appoint replacement LPAC members from time to time.

\(a\) **Advisory Capacity.** The LPAC shall act in an advisory (non-fiduciary) capacity and shall not have the authority to act on behalf of the Partnership or to bind the Partnership or any Partner to any agreement or obligation. LPAC members shall not, by virtue of their service on the LPAC, be deemed to be general partners or to owe fiduciary duties to the Partnership or any Partner.
\(b\) **Matters Requiring LPAC Consent or Consultation.** The following matters shall require the prior consent or consultation of the LPAC, as applicable:
> \(iv\) Consent to the second Extension Period (extending the Fund Term from May 15, 2038 to May 15, 2039);
> \(x\) Such other matters as may be referred to the LPAC by the General Partner from time to time.
\(a\) The LPAC shall meet at least semi-annually (in person, by video conference, or by teleconference) and at any other time upon the request of the General Partner or any two (2) LPAC members.

\(b\) The General Partner shall provide meeting materials (including agendas and relevant supporting documentation) to LPAC members at least five (5) Business Days in advance of each scheduled meeting.

\(c\) A quorum for purposes of LPAC meetings shall consist of a majority of the then-serving LPAC members. Actions may be taken by the LPAC at a duly convened meeting at which a quorum is present or by written consent of the requisite number of LPAC members.
\(a\) Each LPAC member shall have one (1) vote on all matters submitted to the LPAC for approval or consent.

\(b\) Unless otherwise specified in this Agreement, decisions of the LPAC shall be made by a simple majority of the votes cast by LPAC members present (in person or by proxy) at a duly convened meeting or acting by written consent.

\(c\) A supermajority vote (two-thirds of the then-serving LPAC members) shall be required for (i) consent to investments exceeding the Concentration Limit and (ii) consent to acceptance of Aggregate Commitments in excess of the Hard Cap.
**[Section 14.5 --- Indemnification of LPAC Members]{.underline}**

Each LPAC member shall be indemnified by the Partnership to the same extent as the General Partner and other Covered Persons are indemnified under Article XVI. For purposes of Article XVI, LPAC members shall be deemed \"Covered Persons.\"

\(c\) The books and records shall include, without limitation, a copy of this Agreement (as amended from time to time), the Certificate of Limited Partnership, all financial statements, tax returns, the Schedule of Partners, and such other records as are required to be maintained under the DRULPA or applicable law.

\(a\) The Partnership shall indemnify and hold harmless the General Partner, its members, managers, officers, and employees, the Management Company, the LPAC members, and the Affiliates, agents, and representatives of each of the foregoing (collectively, \"Covered Persons\"), from and against any and all losses, claims, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including, without limitation, reasonable attorneys\' fees and expenses, judgments, fines, settlements, and other amounts) (collectively, \"Losses\") arising out of, relating to, or in connection with any act or omission of such Covered Person in connection with the business or affairs of the Partnership; *provided*, *however*, that no Covered Person shall be entitled to indemnification under this Section 16.1 to the extent that such Losses result from the willful misconduct, gross negligence, fraud, or bad faith of such Covered Person.

\(c\) The General Partner shall use commercially reasonable efforts to maintain VCOC status throughout the Fund Term, including by obtaining and exercising management rights in a sufficient number of Portfolio Companies to satisfy the VCOC test.

\(a\) Anti-money laundering (\"AML\") and know-your-customer (\"KYC\") screening of all prospective investors shall be conducted by Halcyon Fund Services, Inc. in accordance with the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act, and applicable regulations promulgated by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (\"FinCEN\").

\(b\) No Side Letter shall contain terms that would materially and adversely affect the rights of other Limited Partners under this Agreement without the prior written consent of such other Limited Partners (or, where applicable, the LPAC).
\(c\) The General Partner shall maintain copies of all Side Letters and shall make them available for review by the LPAC upon request.

\(c\) Notwithstanding the foregoing, the following provisions shall be excluded from MFN elections: (i) fee concessions granted to Limited Partners with Capital Commitments below a specified threshold, (ii) LPAC membership, (iii) provisions specific to the tax status, regulatory requirements, or organizational constraints of the other Limited Partner (e.g., ERISA provisions, FOIA provisions, sovereign immunity provisions), and (iv) such other provisions as the General Partner may reasonably designate as non-MFN provisions.
> \(a\) The expiration of the Fund Term (including any Extension Periods);
> \(c\) The entry of a decree of judicial dissolution of the Partnership under the DRULPA;
> \(i\) the orderly liquidation of all Portfolio Investments in a manner designed to maximize value for the Partners;

Following the completion of the winding up of the Partnership and the distribution of all Partnership assets, the General Partner (or liquidating trustee) shall cause to be filed a Certificate of Cancellation of the Certificate of Limited Partnership with the Secretary of State of the State of Delaware, and shall take such other actions as may be necessary or appropriate to terminate the existence of the Partnership under the DRULPA.
**[Section 20.2 --- Parallel Funds]{.underline}**
\(a\) The General Partner may, in its discretion, establish one or more Parallel Funds to accommodate non-U.S. investors, tax-exempt investors, or investors with specific regulatory requirements.

\(b\) Each Parallel Fund shall invest alongside the Partnership on a pro rata basis (based on the aggregate commitments of the Parallel Fund relative to the aggregate commitments of the Partnership and all Parallel Funds) and on substantially the same economic terms as the Partnership.
\(c\) The General Partner shall be the general partner (or equivalent managing entity) of each Parallel Fund, unless otherwise determined by the General Partner.

\(a\) Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I (Blocker), Inc. may be formed as a Delaware C-Corporation to provide a taxable blocker structure for tax-exempt or non-U.S. investors that wish to avoid unrelated business taxable income (\"UBTI\") or effectively connected income (\"ECI\") that may arise from investments made by the Partnership.

\(a\) This Agreement may be amended, modified, or supplemented by the General Partner with the prior written consent of Limited Partners holding a majority of the aggregate Capital Commitments (excluding the GP Commitment); *provided* that no amendment that would materially and adversely affect the rights of any Limited Partner (including, without limitation, any amendment that would increase such Limited Partner\'s Capital Commitment, reduce such Limited Partner\'s share of distributions, increase the Management Fee, or modify the Carried Interest or Preferred Return) shall be effective without the prior written consent of such Limited Partner.

\(b\) Notwithstanding Section 21.1(a), the General Partner may make administrative, ministerial, or tax-related amendments to this Agreement without Limited Partner consent, including, without limitation, amendments to (i) reflect the admission or withdrawal of Partners, (ii) cure ambiguities or correct errors or omissions, (iii) comply with applicable law, regulation, or court order, or (iv) reflect changes in tax law or regulations that affect the Partnership. This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of Delaware, without regard to the principles of conflict of laws thereof that would require the application of the laws of any other jurisdiction. **RE:** Fund Structure Alternatives and Recommendations --- Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP

The purpose of this memorandum is to present and evaluate the principal fund structuring alternatives available for Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I, LP (\"CLSO Fund I\" or the \"Fund\"), the inaugural opportunistic life-sciences fund to be sponsored by Cobalt Ventures LP (\"Cobalt\" or the \"Sponsor\"). This memorandum analyzes the structural options in light of the Fund\'s anticipated investment strategy, target investor base, economic terms, regulatory requirements, and tax considerations, and provides our recommendations for the preferred fund architecture.

**Recommendation.** Based on our analysis, we recommend that the Fund be organized as a **single-tier Delaware limited partnership** as the primary fund vehicle, supplemented by ancillary structures --- including alternative investment vehicle (\"AIV\") mechanics, a Delaware C-corporation blocker entity, and optional parallel fund or feeder arrangements --- to be deployed on an as-needed basis for specific investor constituencies. This approach provides an institutional-quality structure that is consistent with market practice for life-sciences opportunistic funds at this scale, while preserving maximum flexibility to accommodate the tax, regulatory, and governance requirements of the Fund\'s diverse anticipated investor base.

At the target fund size, this equates to a maximum of approximately \$375,000,000 in platform investments. This limit is appropriate given that platform investments carry different risk characteristics than direct real estate investments, including operational risk, key person dependency, and valuation complexity.
Line 1016: **Leverage Restrictions.** The LPA establishes leverage limits at both the fund and investment level. Fund-level borrowing (exclusive of subscription credit facilities) is limited to a maximum loan-to-value (\"LTV\") ratio of 65% on any individual investment. This is within the standard range for value-add and opportunistic real estate strategies, though it permits a meaningful level of leverage that amplifies both potential returns and potential losses. BFO should be aware that the 65% LTV limit applies on an investment-by-investment basis, not at the fund portfolio level, meaning that the Fund\'s aggregate leverage ratio could exceed 65% if certain investments are leveraged at or near the maximum while others are held with lower or no leverage.
Line 1018: The LPA also permits the GP to enter into subscription credit facilities (also known as capital call facilities or subscription lines of credit) secured by the unfunded Capital Commitments of the Limited Partners. The subscription facility is capped at 25% of aggregate unfunded Capital Commitments, with a maximum outstanding term of 180 days (approximately six months). Subscription facilities are commonly used to bridge the timing gap between investment execution and capital call funding, and they can also be used to fund management fees, organizational expenses, and other Fund Expenses. While subscription facilities provide operational flexibility, BFO should be aware that the use of such facilities can have the effect of enhancing reported IRR by delaying capital calls (thereby reducing the period over which LP capital is deemed invested), even though the total dollar return to LPs is unchanged. BFO should consider requesting additional disclosure regarding the Fund\'s use of subscription facilities in its quarterly reporting.

Line 1036: **A. LPA Baseline**
Line 1038: The base LPA does **not** include a general excuse or exclusion right for Limited Partners. This is a significant gap in the LPA from BFO\'s perspective. In the absence of an excuse right, BFO would be obligated to fund its pro rata share of every capital call issued by the GP during the Investment Period, regardless of the nature of the underlying investment and regardless of any legal, regulatory, or reputational concerns that BFO may have with respect to such investment.
Line 1040: The LPA provides only a narrow regulatory excuse mechanism in Section 4.5, which states that a Limited Partner may be excused from participation in a specific investment if, in the General Partner\'s reasonable determination, such participation would cause the Limited Partner to violate any applicable law or governmental regulation. This provision places the determination of whether a legal or regulatory conflict exists in the hands of the GP, not the affected LP. There is no investor-initiated excuse mechanism, and the GP retains sole discretion over whether to grant an excuse under this narrow provision.
Line 1042: Furthermore, the LPA does not contain any cap on the aggregate amount of investments from which an LP may be excused, because the general excuse right does not exist in the base document. The narrow regulatory excuse in Section 4.5 is treated as an exception to the mandatory capital call provisions rather than as an affirmative LP right.
Line 1044: The absence of a general excuse right is below market standard for institutional real estate PE funds of this size. In our experience, the majority of fund LPAs in the current market environment include some form of excuse or exclusion mechanism, even if it is limited to specified categories of investments and subject to a cap on the aggregate amount of excused investments.
Line 1064: **Cap on Excused Investments.** We anticipate that the GP will seek to impose a cap on the aggregate amount of investments from which BFO may be excused, expressed as a percentage of BFO\'s Capital Commitment. This is standard market practice, as the GP has a legitimate interest in ensuring that each LP funds a meaningful share of the Fund\'s investment portfolio and cannot use the excuse mechanism to effectively reduce its commitment below a minimum threshold.
Line 1066: The typical market range for excuse caps is 10%--25% of an LP\'s Capital Commitment. We recommend that BFO propose a cap of 25%, which would permit BFO to exercise excuse rights with respect to investments aggregating up to \$18,750,000 (\$75,000,000 × 25%). We anticipate that the GP may counter at a lower cap of 15%, which would limit excused investments to \$11,250,000 (\$75,000,000 × 15%). We consider a 15% cap to be acceptable as a fallback position, given the relatively low likelihood that the Fund would make a significant number of investments in the specified categories given its North American commercial real estate focus.

Line 1112: **Triggering Event.** An LP Default is triggered if a Limited Partner fails to fund its pro rata share of a capital call within ten (10) business days of the funding date specified in the capital call notice. This is a hard deadline --- the LPA does not provide for any grace period beyond the 10-business-day notice period already built into the capital call mechanics. However, the LPA does provide for a separate cure period after a default has been triggered.
Line 1118: > \(a\) **Capital Account Forfeiture.** The defaulting LP\'s interest in the Fund is subject to forfeiture of up to 50% of its capital account balance. This is a punitive measure designed to deter defaults and compensate non-defaulting LPs and the Fund for the disruption caused by the default. The 50% forfeiture rate is at the high end of the market range, which typically falls between 25% and 50%. We note that a 50% forfeiture on BFO\'s \$75,000,000 commitment could represent a forfeiture of up to \$37,500,000 of capital account value (assuming BFO\'s full commitment has been called and funded at the time of the default), which would constitute a catastrophic loss.

The LPA provides that the prevailing party in any such proceeding shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs from the non-prevailing party.
Line 1126: We note that the LPA does not include a \"pay-to-play\" or interest downgrade mechanism as an alternative to outright forfeiture. In some fund LPAs, a defaulting LP\'s interest is converted from a full participating interest to a non-voting, non-participating interest (sometimes referred to as a \"penalty box\" or \"zombie\" interest), which reduces the defaulting LP\'s economic rights but does not result in outright forfeiture of capital. The absence of such an intermediate remedy in Fund IV\'s LPA means that the consequences of a default are binary --- either the LP cures the default within the cure period, or it faces the full suite of punitive consequences described above.

Recommendation.** While the default remedies in the LPA are aggressive, they are within the range of market practice for institutional PE funds and serve the legitimate purpose of deterring defaults and protecting the Fund and non-defaulting LPs from the consequences of an LP\'s failure to fund. We advise BFO to ensure that it maintains adequate liquidity and operational procedures to timely fund all capital calls issued by the GP throughout the life of the Fund.
Line 1130: We do not recommend side-letter negotiation on the default remedies provisions. In our experience, the GP is unlikely to agree to modifications to the default provisions for a single LP, as the uniformity of default remedies across all LPs is important for the structural integrity of the Fund and the GP\'s ability to manage LP defaults consistently. BFO should instead focus its attention on establishing robust internal processes for monitoring and responding to capital call notices within the required funding periods.
Line 1134: **A. LPA Baseline**
Line 1136: The LPA imposes significant restrictions on the transferability of LP interests. The key transfer provisions are as follows:
Line 1138: **General Prohibition.** LP interests in the Fund are not transferable without the prior written consent of the General Partner. The GP may grant or withhold such consent in its sole and absolute discretion, and the GP is not required to provide any reason or basis for withholding consent. This is a broad restriction that effectively gives the GP a veto right over any proposed transfer.
Line 1140: **Affiliate Transfer Exception.** The LPA provides a limited exception for transfers to affiliates of the transferring LP. An LP may transfer all or a portion of its interest to an \"affiliate\" (as defined in the LPA) without GP consent, provided that: (i) the transferring LP provides the GP with at least 30 days\' prior written notice of the proposed transfer, (ii) the GP\'s consent to the transfer is obtained (which consent may not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed), and (iii) the transferee affiliate executes a joinder agreement and becomes bound by all provisions of the LPA. We note that, while the LPA states that GP consent for affiliate transfers may not be \"unreasonably withheld,\" this standard still provides the GP with meaningful discretion to block a proposed transfer on reasonable grounds.
Line 1142: **Transfers by Operation of Law.** The LPA recognizes transfers by operation of law (e.g., in connection with a merger, estate administration, or court order) as an exception to the general transfer restriction, provided that the transferee complies with applicable securities laws and the other requirements of the LPA.
Line 1144: **General Conditions.** Any transfer of an LP interest, whether pursuant to the general consent requirement, the affiliate exception, or by operation of law, must satisfy the following conditions: (i) the transfer must comply with all applicable federal and state securities laws, including the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, and applicable state blue sky laws; (ii) the transfer must not cause the Fund to be treated as a \"publicly traded partnership\" within the meaning of Section 7704 of the Internal Revenue Code; and (iii) the transfer must not cause any material adverse tax consequence to the Fund or any other Limited Partner, as determined by the GP in consultation with the Fund\'s tax advisors.
Line 1146: The LPA does not include a right of first refusal in favor of other Limited Partners --- that is, existing LPs do not have the right to purchase a transferring LP\'s interest before it is transferred to a third party. Additionally, the LPA does not include drag-along or tag-along rights, which would be unusual for a limited partnership fund of this type.

Line 1152: For purposes of the side letter, \"Hargrove Family Entity\" should be defined broadly to include: (i) any trust or estate established for the benefit of one or more members of the Hargrove family (defined to include Julian Hargrove, his spouse, his lineal descendants, and any trust or estate for the primary benefit of any such person); (ii) any limited partnership, limited liability company, or other entity wholly owned or controlled (directly or indirectly) by one or more members of the Hargrove family; and (iii) any charitable foundation or donor-advised fund established by one or more members of the Hargrove family. The definition should be drafted with sufficient breadth to accommodate BFO\'s current estate planning structure as well as any future changes to the Hargrove family\'s wealth planning arrangements.
Line 1154: This provision addresses BFO\'s estate planning and family wealth structuring needs, which may require the transfer of BFO\'s LP interest to one or more family trusts, holding companies, or other entities during the life of the Fund. These conditions are reasonable and should be acceptable to BFO.

Line 1162: The LPA provides for the formation of a Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\") composed of representatives of five to seven (5--7) Limited Partners. LPAC members are selected by the General Partner from among the Fund\'s largest investors.
