The dormancy arises in the context of a Material Impediment Event triggered by the Portland Metropolitan Water District\'s October 28, 2022 notice to Cascadia Renewables Holdings, Inc. (\"Cascadia\" or \"CRH\") of its intent to renegotiate the Bull Run Filtration Project 40-year water-treatment concession. That concession, originally executed in 2018, generates annual revenue of approximately \$64 million and represents a material component of Cascadia\'s long-term contracted revenue base. The Water District\'s notice cited changed regulatory requirements arising from Oregon Senate Bill 1567 (2022), which imposed new water-treatment standards and recalibrated the regulatory framework governing municipal water-service concessions throughout the state.

The underlying acquisition of Cascadia by Cascadia Acquisition Corp. --- a special-purpose acquisition entity to be owned by Meridian Infrastructure Partners Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\") and the Co-Invest --- has stalled as a result. The Equity Purchase Agreement (the \"EPA\"), originally executed on September 15, 2022, provided for an outside date of December 31, 2022. Pursuant to the First Amendment to the EPA, dated November 22, 2022, the outside date was extended to March 31, 2023. Further extensions remain possible but are not assured, and would require the agreement of the selling shareholders, Cascadia, and the buyer party, with implications for the co-invest structure discussed herein.

This memorandum addresses five principal areas of analysis: (A) Ironside\'s rights during dormancy, including information rights, consent rights, the wind-down election right, and rights under the EPA and ancillary transaction documents; (B) Ironside\'s continuing obligations, including entity maintenance, unfunded commitment exposure, and cooperation duties; (C) the GP\'s duties and constraints during dormancy, including fiduciary obligations, expense management, and the prohibition on affirmative investment activity; (D) Ironside\'s financial exposure during dormancy, including an analysis of capital deployed, estimated dormancy operating expenses, opportunity costs, and R&W insurance and debt commitment considerations; and (E) the strategic options available to Ironside, ranging from passive monitoring to active engagement, negotiated exit, wind-down election, and potential transaction restructuring.

These consent rights are critical in the current environment. Sections 5.03 and 7.04 of the LP Agreement clearly require the LP\'s prior written consent for any new capital calls during a Material Impediment Event dormancy period. Under the LP Agreement and the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act (\"DRULPA\"), 6 Del. C. §§ 17-101 *et seq.*, the GP owes fiduciary duties to the Vehicle and to Ironside as the LP. The LP Agreement modifies but does not eliminate these duties; it specifies that the GP must act in good faith and in a manner that the GP reasonably believes to be in the best interests of the partnership.

During dormancy, the GP may authorize the payment of ordinary-course operating expenses of the Vehicle, including fund administration fees, audit and tax compliance costs, Delaware franchise taxes, registered agent fees, and similar recurring expenses. > \(a\) the failure, or expected failure, of a condition precedent to the closing of the Target Acquisition (as defined in the LP Agreement) that is not reasonably likely to be cured or satisfied within ninety (90) days following the date of the GP\'s determination (herein, \"**Prong (a)**\"); or

Prong (a) focuses on the closing conditions of the underlying acquisition. To invoke this prong, the GP must determine that a condition precedent to closing has failed or is expected to fail, and that such failure is not reasonably likely to be cured or satisfied within 90 days of the GP\'s determination.

**Identification of the Relevant Closing Condition.** The EPA contains a number of conditions to the obligation of the Buyer (Cascadia Acquisition Corp.) to consummate the Acquisition at closing. Among the most significant of these is the representation bring-down condition, which requires that the representations and warranties of the Selling Shareholders and the Target set forth in the EPA shall be true and correct in all material respects as of the closing date. In particular, Article VII, Section 7.02(a) of the EPA includes a condition that, since the date of the EPA, no Material Adverse Effect shall have occurred with respect to Cascadia (the \"**no-MAE closing condition**\"). The satisfaction of this condition is a prerequisite to the Buyer\'s obligation to close.

While C&H\'s prior memorandum dated November 14, 2022 analyzed this question in detail and concluded that certain carve-outs in the EPA\'s MAE definition --- including, in particular, the regulatory-change exception in clause (iv) of the MAE carve-outs and the industry-wide developments exception in clause (ii) --- may apply to shield the concession renegotiation from constituting a MAE, the application of those carve-outs is fact-intensive and subject to reasonable disagreement. The GP may reasonably take the position that the concession renegotiation constitutes, or is reasonably expected to result in, a Material Adverse Effect, and that accordingly the no-MAE closing condition is expected to fail.

We note that the GP need not establish with certainty that the no-MAE closing condition *will* fail --- Prong (a) requires only the \"expected failure\" of the condition, a standard that contemplates a reasonable assessment of future events rather than a definitive determination. Under Delaware law, the GP\'s determination is subject to a reasonableness standard, and the GP is afforded a degree of discretion in making this assessment so long as it acts in good faith and on a reasonable basis. Given the magnitude of the Bull Run Concession to Cascadia\'s revenue, the uncertainty surrounding the renegotiation outcome, and the substantive arguments on both sides of the MAE carve-out analysis, the GP\'s determination that the no-MAE closing condition is \"expected\" to fail is within the range of reasonable determinations.

**Pending OPUC Approval.** In addition to the no-MAE closing condition, the EPA contains a regulatory-approval closing condition requiring, among other things, the receipt of approval from the Oregon Public Utility Commission. As noted in Section III.D above, the OPUC application (Docket No. UM-2287) was filed on October 14, 2022 and remains pending. No order or interim ruling has been issued. Whether the absence of OPUC approval independently constitutes a failure of a closing condition is arguable --- the condition has not technically \"failed\" but rather remains unsatisfied --- but the concession renegotiation has effectively stalled the regulatory process, and there is no basis for confidence that OPUC approval will be obtained within any particular timeframe. The pending OPUC application provides additional support for the GP\'s position that closing conditions are at risk of not being satisfied.

**Conclusion on Prong (a):** The GP has a reasonable basis to conclude that the expected failure of the no-MAE closing condition satisfies Prong (a) of the Material Impediment Event definition. The concession renegotiation and its uncertain outcome make the no-MAE condition unlikely to be satisfied, the pending OPUC approval provides further support, and cure within 90 days is not reasonably likely given the complexity and current trajectory of the negotiations. We are satisfied that the GP\'s reliance on Prong (a) is substantively sound.

This prong requires an *actual* occurrence of a Material Adverse Effect, as distinguished from the *expected failure* of a closing condition under Prong (a). The standard is therefore more demanding: the GP must be in a position to assert that a MAE has in fact occurred, not merely that one may be expected.

The GP need not rely exclusively on Prong (b) if Prong (a) is satisfied. However, the factual basis for the declaration is strengthened by the interconnection between the two prongs: the same set of circumstances (the concession renegotiation) gives rise to both the expected failure of the no-MAE closing condition under Prong (a) and the potential occurrence of a Material Adverse Effect under Prong (b).

**Conclusion on Prong (b):** There is a colorable but less certain basis for the GP\'s declaration under Prong (b). The stronger basis for the declaration rests on Prong (a), which requires only the \"expected failure\" of a closing condition rather than the actual occurrence of a MAE. We note, however, that the GP\'s draft Capital Call Suspension Notice cites only Prong (a) as the basis for the declaration, which is the more defensible approach.

Based on the foregoing analysis, the GP\'s anticipated declaration of a Material Impediment Event has a sound substantive basis under Section 7.04(a) of the LP Agreement. The declaration is primarily grounded in Prong (a) --- the expected failure of the no-MAE closing condition, which is not reasonably likely to be cured within 90 days --- and this basis is well-supported by the factual record. The concession renegotiation, its uncertain outcome, the pending OPUC approval, and the impracticability of resolution within the 90-day period collectively provide a reasonable foundation for the GP\'s determination.

**Description of Matter.** This matter involves the representation of a single-family office client, Briarwood Family Office LLC, in connection with the review, drafting, and negotiation of a side letter to the limited partnership agreement of Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P., a Delaware limited partnership. The engagement encompasses all activities related to the client\'s proposed limited partnership commitment to the fund, including subscription documentation review, side-letter negotiation with the fund\'s general partner and its outside counsel, and advisory services regarding fund terms, economics, and governance provisions. The matter has been assigned to the Funds & Asset Management practice group and will be staffed principally out of the firm\'s New York office.

He is the principal decision-maker for all investment activities of the family office and holds veto authority over the client\'s Investment Committee. We note that the absence of any LP consent requirement for the extension periods is a less favorable term from BFO\'s perspective. While the first one-year extension at GP discretion is consistent with common market practice, there is an increasing trend in the institutional private equity market to require some form of investor consent for the second extension year --- typically either (i) approval by the Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\"), or (ii) a vote of a majority or super-majority of Limited Partners. The rationale for such a requirement is that a second extension indicates potential difficulty in realizing the Fund\'s remaining portfolio, and LPs should have a voice in determining whether continued management by the GP is in the best interests of the Fund.

The General Partner is required to fund its own GP Capital Commitment on a pari passu basis with the Limited Partners --- that is, the GP must fund its pro rata share of each capital call at the same time and in the same proportion as the Limited Partners. The GP\'s Capital Commitment is established in the LPA at 1.0% of aggregate Capital Commitments. At the target fund size of \$1,500,000,000, the GP\'s anticipated commitment would be \$15,000,000. This 1.0% GP commitment is standard for the market, though we note that some institutional investors prefer a GP commitment in the range of 1.5%--3.0% to ensure stronger alignment of interest between the GP and the LPs. BFO may wish to consider this point in its broader investment evaluation, though we do not recommend it as a side-letter negotiation item as it is unlikely to be modified for a single investor.

The LPA defines the Fund\'s investment strategy as the pursuit of value-add and opportunistic investments in North American commercial real estate, real estate operating companies, and asset management platforms. This is a broad investment mandate that encompasses a wide range of real estate asset types, including office, multifamily, industrial, retail, hospitality, and specialty asset classes, as well as investments in operating platforms that manage or develop real estate assets.

The LPA identifies two individuals as \"Key Persons\" for purposes of the Fund\'s key person provisions: (i) Conrad J. Their continued involvement is a critical element of BFO\'s investment thesis for Fund IV.
**A. Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC)**

The LPA provides for the formation of a Limited Partner Advisory Committee (\"LPAC\") composed of representatives of five to seven (5--7) Limited Partners. LPAC members are selected by the General Partner from among the Fund\'s largest investors. The LPA does not specify a minimum commitment threshold for LPAC membership but states that the GP will \"endeavor to select LPAC members from among the Fund\'s most significant investors.\"

Fund IV is organized as a Delaware limited partnership and is treated as a partnership for U.S. federal income tax purposes. As a partnership, Fund IV is not subject to entity-level federal income tax; instead, each partner (including each LP) is taxed on its allocable share of the Fund\'s income, gain, loss, deduction, and credit items, as reported on the annual Schedule K-1. This pass-through tax structure is the standard structure for institutional PE funds and is appropriate for BFO.

{"file_path":"response.md","content":"# Funds & Asset Management matters involving an LP advisory committee

## Answer

**4 matters.** I counted a matter when (1) it is a Funds & Asset Management matter (including the earlier **Private Funds** practice designation), (2) the fund or co-investment vehicle in the matter had an LP advisory committee or an equivalent committee of LP representatives, and (3) the governing LPA was an existing/executed agreement—not merely a draft for a proposed fundraise. I treated the **Investor Advisory Committee (IAC)** in Matter 1024-00002 as the functional equivalent of an LP advisory committee because it is a committee of the fund’s limited partners established under the LPA.

## Matters counted

| Matter | Fund / vehicle | Why it qualifies | LPA execution check | Key documents relied on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1001-00002** | **Ardent Capital Partners III LP (Fund III)** | The matter’s conflict memorandum assigns the team to the **Private Funds** practice and describes an LPAC-consent workstream. The matter closing memorandum says Fund III’s LPAC had four members representing significant LPs. The LPAC notification/consent letter and presentation memorandum document the February 14, 2024 LPAC meeting and consent. | The Fund was an existing 2019 fund with an existing A&R LPA. The closing memorandum records that **Amendment No. 1 to the LPA was executed February 28, 2024**, after LPAC consent. This is not a never-signed LPA. | `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/conflict-check-memo.docx` — Private Funds staffing and LPAC-consent scope; `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-notification-and-consent-letter.docx` — solicitation of LPAC consent under LPA §9.4; `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-presentation-memo.docx` — materials for the Fund III LPAC; `documents/matters/1001-00002/Amended Governing Documents/lpa-amendment-no-1.docx` — executed LPA amendment; `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/matter-closing-memo.docx` — confirms all restructuring documents were executed and records the LPAC consent and LPA amendment. |
| **1024-00002** | **Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd. (DARF)** | DARF had a five-member **Investor Advisory Committee (IAC)** under LPA §9.02. The engagement concerned a Key Person Event, successor governance, LP consents, and an LPA amendment; the IAC reviewed the proposal and recommended approval. | The engagement letter identifies the existing A&R LPA as dated **March 15, 2017**. The closing certificate records that the required consents were received and that the First Amendment became effective **August 26, 2024**; the closing memorandum states the execution version was signed and the matter was completed. | `documents/matters/1024-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-darf-gp-advisory.docx` — Funds & Asset Management engagement and existing A&R LPA; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Analyses & Memos/iac-presentation-memo.docx` — IAC composition, role, and review meeting; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Transaction Documents/execution-first-amendment-ar-lpa.docx` — execution version of the LPA amendment; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Closing/closing-certificate-consent-tabulation.docx` — 38 of 47 LP consents (86.2%) and August 26 effectiveness; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Closing/engagement-closing-memo.docx` — confirms completion and execution. |
| **1026-00001** | **Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P.** | The intake memorandum expressly assigns the matter to the **Funds & Asset Management** practice. The LPA review memorandum states that Fund IV’s LPA provides for a Limited Partner Advisory Committee of five to seven LP representatives and analyzes its authority and composition. | The fund LPA was an existing A&R LPA dated **December 20, 2023**, supplied as the Fund’s governing document and reviewed provision-by-provision. The client later declined the proposed commitment, so the proposed side letter and subscription agreement were never executed; that does **not** mean Fund IV’s own LPA was unsigned. The closing memorandum expressly distinguishes the unexecuted client documents from the existing Fund IV LPA. | `documents/matters/1026-00001/Engagement & Administration/engagement-letter.docx` — identifies Fund IV’s dated A&R LPA and F&AM practice assignment; `documents/matters/1026-00001/LPA & PPM Review/lpa-review-memorandum.docx` — LPAC composition and authority; `documents/matters/1026-00001/LPA & PPM Review/ppm-summary-risk-assessment.docx` — LPAC/key-person analysis; `documents/matters/1026-00001/Engagement & Administration/matter-closing-memorandum.docx` — confirms the client passed and only the side-letter/subscription work remained unsigned. |
| **1027-00002** | **Ridgeline-Clarion Co-Invest, L.P.**, co-investing alongside Ridgeline Equity Partners Fund IV, L.P. | This is a Funds & Asset Management matter. The co-invest vehicle’s LPA establishes a three-member LPAC, and the side letter gives Pellegrino the right to designate one LPAC member. | The execution-version LPA states it was entered into and effective **January 30, 2026**. The closing checklist records the LPA and side letter as fully executed on January 30, 2026. | `documents/matters/1027-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-pellegrino.docx` — F&AM engagement and LPAC-seat workstream; `documents/matters/1027-00002/Transaction Documents/co-invest-lpa-execution-version.docx` — effective LPA and Article IX LPAC; `documents/matters/1027-00002/Transaction Documents/side-letter-pellegrino.docx` — Pellegrino’s LPAC-seat right; `documents/matters/1027-00002/Closing/closing-checklist.xlsx` — execution/closing evidence. |

## Exclusions and application of the signed-LPA filter

- **1002-00003 — Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP:** the matter documents describe the LPA as expected to be dated at the future First Close and the side-letter program as part of a future fundraise. The advisory-committee seat was prospective; no signed fund LPA was established in the reviewed record.
- **1003-00002 — Harrowgate Private Equity Fund V LP:** the LPA, LPAC Charter, and parallel-fund documents are expressly drafts tied to a target First Close of August 15, 2025. The initial LPA says it is for discussion purposes and non-binding. Excluded.
- **1004-00002 — Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I LP:** the first LPA is expressly a confidential draft, with the First Close targeted for November 15, 2026; its LPAC provisions were prospective. Excluded.
- **1002-00005 — Pinnacle Continuation Vehicle LP:** the LPAC language appears in a tax markup and proposed CV materials, including a closing certificate stated to be completed and executed at closing. The CV LPA was still a draft with a target October 31, 2025 closing, so it does not satisfy the signed-LPA requirement. The matter also appears as a Tax practice engagement rather than a Funds & Asset Management matter.
- **1023-00001 — ICM Cascadia Co-Invest, LP:** although the LP Agreement was ultimately executed, the formation/governance memorandum expressly states that **no formal LPAC was established** because the vehicle had a single limited partner; direct consultation and consent rights substituted for an LPAC. Excluded on the committee criterion.
- **1041-00005 — Solara fund-platform reorganization:** the records identify LPACs for existing Solara funds, but this is a Tax/PLR engagement, not a Funds & Asset Management matter. It is therefore outside the requested practice-group population.

Accordingly, after applying both the practice-group scope and the requirement that the relevant LPA be signed/existing, the staffing count is **4 matters**."}

lines.text: # Funds & Asset Management matters involving an LP advisory committee
## Answer

**4 matters.** I counted a matter when (1) it is a Funds & Asset Management matter (including the earlier **Private Funds** practice designation), (2) the fund or co-investment vehicle in the matter had an LP advisory committee or an equivalent committee of LP representatives, and (3) the governing LPA was an existing/executed agreement—not merely a draft for a proposed fundraise. I treated the **Investor Advisory Committee (IAC)** in Matter 1024-00002 as the functional equivalent of an LP advisory committee because it is a committee of the fund’s limited partners established under the LPA.
## Matters counted
| Matter | Fund / vehicle | Why it qualifies | LPA execution check | Key documents relied on |

| **1001-00002** | **Ardent Capital Partners III LP (Fund III)** | The matter’s conflict memorandum assigns the team to the **Private Funds** practice and describes an LPAC-consent workstream. The matter closing memorandum says Fund III’s LPAC had four members representing significant LPs. The LPAC notification/consent letter and presentation memorandum document the February 14, 2024 LPAC meeting and consent. | The Fund was an existing 2019 fund with an existing A&R LPA. The closing memorandum records that **Amendment No. 1 to the LPA was executed February 28, 2024**, after LPAC consent. This is not a never-signed LPA. | `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/conflict-check-memo.docx` — Private Funds staffing and LPAC-consent scope; `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-notification-and-consent-letter.docx` — solicitation of LPAC consent under LPA §9.4; `documents/matters/1001-00002/LP Consent & Notification/lpac-presentation-memo.docx` — materials for the Fund III LPAC; `documents/matters/1001-00002/Amended Governing Documents/lpa-amendment-no-1.docx` — executed LPA amendment; `documents/matters/1001-00002/Engagement & Administration/matter-closing-memo.docx` — confirms all restructuring documents were executed and records the LPAC consent and LPA amendment. |

| **1024-00002** | **Driftwood Absolute Return Fund Ltd. (DARF)** | DARF had a five-member **Investor Advisory Committee (IAC)** under LPA §9.02. The engagement concerned a Key Person Event, successor governance, LP consents, and an LPA amendment; the IAC reviewed the proposal and recommended approval. | The engagement letter identifies the existing A&R LPA as dated **March 15, 2017**. The closing certificate records that the required consents were received and that the First Amendment became effective **August 26, 2024**; the closing memorandum states the execution version was signed and the matter was completed. | `documents/matters/1024-00002/Engagement/engagement-letter-darf-gp-advisory.docx` — Funds & Asset Management engagement and existing A&R LPA; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Analyses & Memos/iac-presentation-memo.docx` — IAC composition, role, and review meeting; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Transaction Documents/execution-first-amendment-ar-lpa.docx` — execution version of the LPA amendment; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Closing/closing-certificate-consent-tabulation.docx` — 38 of 47 LP consents (86.2%) and August 26 effectiveness; `documents/matters/1024-00002/Closing/engagement-closing-memo.docx` — confirms completion and execution. |

| **1026-00001** | **Meridian Peak Capital Partners Fund IV, L.P.** | The intake memorandum expressly assigns the matter to the **Funds & Asset Management** practice. The LPA review memorandum states that Fund IV’s LPA provides for a Limited Partner Advisory Committee of five to seven LP representatives and analyzes its authority and composition. | The fund LPA was an existing A&R LPA dated **December 20, 2023**, supplied as the Fund’s governing document and reviewed provision-by-provision. The client later declined the proposed commitment, so the proposed side letter and subscription agreement were never executed; that does **not** mean Fund IV’s own LPA was unsigned. ## Exclusions and application of the signed-LPA filter

- **1002-00003 — Pinnacle Venture Fund II LP:** the matter documents describe the LPA as expected to be dated at the future First Close and the side-letter program as part of a future fundraise. The advisory-committee seat was prospective; no signed fund LPA was established in the reviewed record.

- **1003-00002 — Harrowgate Private Equity Fund V LP:** the LPA, LPAC Charter, and parallel-fund documents are expressly drafts tied to a target First Close of August 15, 2025. The initial LPA says it is for discussion purposes and non-binding. Excluded.

- **1004-00002 — Cobalt Life Sciences Opportunities Fund I LP:** the first LPA is expressly a confidential draft, with the First Close targeted for November 15, 2026; its LPAC provisions were prospective. Excluded.

The CV LPA was still a draft with a target October 31, 2025 closing, so it does not satisfy the signed-LPA requirement. The matter also appears as a Tax practice engagement rather than a Funds & Asset Management matter.

Excluded on the committee criterion.

- **1041-00005 — Solara fund-platform reorganization:** the records identify LPACs for existing Solara funds, but this is a Tax/PLR engagement, not a Funds & Asset Management matter. It is therefore outside the requested practice-group population.
Accordingly, after applying both the practice-group scope and the requirement that the relevant LPA be signed/existing, the staffing count is **4 matters**.
